Any retained callback vetoes a new reservation under shared admission; a callback does not itself grant resend authority, even if it reports failure. A reservation serialized before the callback still represents an already admitted possible external call. This gives operators a truthful audit trail while avoiding causal claims based on untrusted event time.

followups.question: Why authenticate before checking duplicate event ID?
followups.answer: Every retry authenticates its exact current raw bytes before receipt lookup. A provider may re-sign with a fresh timestamp or reorder JSON while preserving the canonical eight-field observation. That replay is allowed; changing state, occurredAt or providerMessageId under the same event conflicts.

followups.question: What if delivered arrives before accepted?
followups.answer: Keep the observations and apply the deterministic provider-specific evidence rule. Network arrival order and provider timestamps do not define business authority. A stronger reported state may be useful evidence while contradictions remain visible rather than being erased.

chapter_title: P2 One conversation across channels
title: A stable receiver accepts the original result
question: How does a P3 result become a P2 notice without confusing the result digest with the message body?
answer: ChannelResultReceiver is constructed with a retained receiver UUID and finite trusted publisher bindings. Accept and find require a distinct publisher capability scoped to the account, case, conversation and logical recipient. The original canonical P1 delivery intent fixes delivery, work, attempt and result digest. Exact replay returns the same receipt; changed intent conflicts. The receiver ID cannot rotate on serving startup or be borrowed from an unrelated ordinary outbox row.

Under the existing outbox admission lock and maxReplies cap, result metadata and a fixed ordinary notice commit together. The notice's bodyDigest describes the notice text; it is not the P1 result_sha256. The retained canonical intent includes the base64 result body; the ordinary notice contains separate fixed text. Receiver acceptance is an application receipt that the result was retained at this explicit receiver. It grants no carrier send, physical hearing, human acknowledgement or business action. The real storage fixture tests atomic acceptance, concurrent replay, changed and foreign data denial, ordinary UUID collision, full opaque result separation and populated restore. These are separate from later current-native disclosure.

followups.question: Why retain a receiver UUID rather than generate one per process?
followups.answer: P1 binds delivery to its original receiver before the first send. A restart must reconcile the same receiver identity. Rotating it would either make original receipts unreachable or silently redirect an ambiguous delivery to a new receiver.

followups.question: Can a result receipt be returned when maxReplies is full?
followups.answer: Exact replay and read remain available because they do not add protected identity. New acceptance still obeys the cap. Checking replay before growth prevents overload from blocking reconciliation of a result already accepted.

chapter_title: P2 One conversation across channels
title: Disclose an old result through a current grant
question: How can a new room read an old result while still enforcing the current participant permission?
answer: ChannelResultReader derives the route from the current native grant and verifies that its inbox and outbox refer to the same configured database identity. It takes a bounded P2 observation of the original result under the stable receiver, releases SQL, calls the exact public P1 case adapter, then rechecks the original native grant under locks with fresh database time. The final check compares binding, room, participant and full logical reference before disclosing the result.

One shared outbox call slot stays owned across the entire sequence, even though no connection or transaction spans the external read. The returned intent and receipt retain original identities; the accompanying case and observation times are separate as-of facts with atomic false. If permission is lost while P1 is being read, disclosure is denied rather than returning the earlier snapshot. A first genuine denial must still release the slot so a later authorized read can progress. This is a read boundary only: an old result becoming visible through a fresh room does not create a new generation, resend, consent or action permission.

followups.question: Why retain the call slot while releasing the SQL connection?
followups.answer: The slot bounds the complete read, including the external case adapter; the SQL connection only bounds its database stages. The denial-then-success test requires both reader.active and storageActive to return to zero. Otherwise correct denial could still become a permanent availability failure.

followups.question: Does the final check make the result current?
followups.answer: It makes disclosure admitted under the original current grant at that final point. P1 and P2 remain separate timed observations, and the result's applicability must still be interpreted against them. It does not make a cross-store atomic snapshot.

chapter_title: P2 One conversation across channels
title: Schema changes belong to the owner
question: Why are inbox upgrades explicit, and what do versions five through nine actually change?
answer: Serving code uses a restricted runtime role and performs no DDL. The trusted owner upgrades a quiescent selected schema through explicit versioned functions, preserving original identities and old API behavior. v5 adds immutable provider operations and recovery metadata, adopting all old attempts as ordinary. v6 adds native grants, v7 adds communication evidence, and v8 adds original P1 result receipts linked to ordinary notices. These are distinct storage capabilities rather than one automatic startup migration.

v9 adds three operating indexes for due dispatch, provider-operation attempts and outbound recovery commands; it changes no business row; version, digest and catalog metadata do change. The latest audit added explicit locks around that maintenance upgrade. Compatibility means older upgrade functions do not downgrade newer schemas, source and installed consumers keep original receipt semantics, and populated backup/restore/reopen procedures are exercised. I would discuss the operational price honestly: quiescent owner upgrades require a maintenance procedure, but make privilege and data transitions reviewable. Installing schema in a library constructor would hide irreversible work in ordinary serving startup and weaken the separation between trusted administration and request handling.

followups.question: Why not infer idempotent capability while migrating old attempts?
followups.answer: The old external call was made under its original contract. A migration cannot manufacture a provider guarantee after the fact. Preserve it as ordinary and require explicit semantics for future new operations.

followups.question: How do you validate an index-only migration?
followups.answer: Verify the expected source version and owner role, protected maintenance locks, exact new index definitions, unchanged logical row snapshots, idempotent original reopen behavior and compatibility reads. Faster queries alone do not prove the upgrade preserved history.

chapter_title: P2 One conversation across channels
title: Original input provenance survives the bridge
question: Why did the joined application need an operation-only client instead of pretending native text was SMS?
answer: The operation-only ExternalOperationClient overload takes a trusted profile, loopback endpoint, finite account/case/conversation/sender binding and operation bearer. It does not require synthetic carrier configuration for a native publisher. The original canonical channel input stays in P2; the application bridge returns the actual P1 work UUID as its external receipt. A kind label or receipt shape alone cannot prove whether an operation originated from native text or signed SMS.

The qualified source join follows the retained accepted event through its exact prepared operation to the original P1 work and result. Mapped P3 identifiers are restricted at the bridge without narrowing unrelated P2-only event and sender bounds. Closed descriptors and independent encoded-frame and canonical-input limits are checked before I/O. The old two-argument client remains compatible. An accept error stays OutcomeUnknown while a failed lookup stays Unavailable; neither authorizes choosing another operation key. The latest audit aligned the joined client call budget with the five-second step while preserving the default two-second budget for existing consumers. This is an example of improving composition without broadening authority.

followups.question: Why is a returned work UUID not enough to prove origin?
followups.answer: A valid UUID only identifies some work. Prove the join from the authenticated original receipt and operation through canonical preparation to that P1 record. The pure fixture validates source UUID distinctness; actual provenance needs the separate accepted-event/P1 integration evidence, not that parser test alone.

followups.question: Where should unsupported IDs be rejected?
followups.answer: At the explicit integration seam that maps into the narrower P3 contract. Reject without truncation or rewriting. A bridge limitation should not silently shrink the standalone channel SDK's existing valid input space.

chapter_title: P2 One conversation across channels
title: Operations pages are bounded readers
question: What makes the operations view safe to expose, and how do its cursors work?
answer: The operations API is a scoped read model, with independent operator diagnostics and no mutation or resend control. Context reads still use the native permission and final disclosure checks. Signed cursors bind application source, full logical scope, section and retained anchor; they are pagination state, not authentication. HMAC verification and anchor validation prevent one section or profile's cursor from being replayed against another, and an incompatible case-source revision returns cursor_stale.

Telemetry uses finite producer maps, metric names and error vocabularies. Bodies, tokens and arbitrary labels are excluded; failed getters are unavailable rather than substituted with zero. Exporters and observers are bounded and owned before invoking callbacks or thenable access, including reentrant close and ignored asynchronous work. This matters because diagnostics themselves can leak resources or block ordinary useful work. The tests retain actual returned promises through incomplete close, verify later settlement, and separate caller-span completion from real reader ownership. An accepted-row page is also not a complete status-event feed: explicit refresh and separately timed observations remain part of the UI contract.

followups.question: Why is a signed cursor not authorization?
followups.answer: It authenticates pagination state, not the reader. Every page still needs current permission. The cursor binds the case source fingerprint as well as scope and section; workflow/supplier changes can stale it even when the request revision is unchanged. A matching revision is not a freshness exemption.

followups.question: Why report a failed metric as unavailable rather than zero?
followups.answer: Zero is a real measurement and can falsely imply healthy inactivity. Unavailable preserves the observation failure. Bounded enums and source ownership also keep exporter errors from introducing untrusted labels or leaking private exception text.

chapter_title: P2 One conversation across channels
title: A workload is evidence within a declared envelope
question: What did the P2 workload study measure, and what would be an overclaim?
answer: The selected workload freezes its manifest, digest, schedules, seeds, child roles, cleanup and numeric ceilings before measurement. It exercises fake-SMS intake, persisted processing, duplicate and changed-payload behavior, overload, restart, populated restore and dormant conversations through public ports. The active schedule fills a sixty-four-input retained-capacity profile; the dormant study admits 1,000 inputs under a 1,024-row cap through bounded public credential windows. These are local synthetic workload shapes, not production customer counts.

The study records sampled process RSS, CPU, event-loop delay and latency observations with explicit denominators. Its ceilings include 512 MiB RSS, 1,000 ms maximum observed event-loop delay, 5,000 ms accepted admission and 15,000 ms useful fake-operation completion. Crossing a ceiling fails that profile; passing does not establish a production SLO or fair scheduling. Two gateways share one Node process, so RSS includes both and the runtime baseline. Restarts and restore must preserve original receipts, body conflicts and operation keys. The latest audit records an initial workload timeout under host load and its isolated rerun, which should be described as observed evidence rather than erased.

followups.question: Can you divide total RSS by conversations to estimate production capacity?
followups.answer: Not reliably from this experiment. Runtime baseline, shared pools, active versus dormant work and sampling all affect memory. Build a separate controlled study with the production workload, resource limits, steady state, tail behavior and failure recovery before making capacity claims.

followups.question: Why prove cleanup as part of a benchmark?
followups.answer: Leaked children, held SQL sessions or unresolved observer work can contaminate the measurements and the next run. A pass requires reconciling actual results and owned resources, not merely producing an attractive latency percentile.

chapter_title: P2 One conversation across channels
title: A clean SDK includes honest release boundaries
question: How would you defend the package design, test strategy and remaining P2 work to a framework team?
answer: The package exposes typed subpaths for codec, security, storage, dispatch, routing, confirmation, outbox, native composition, rehydration, operations and result reception. Construction keeps trusted capabilities explicit, public errors use finite safe codes, runtime data is validated, and resources have owned close methods. The installed starter composes these APIs while staying inert on import; owner bootstrap and serving are distinct. Isolated npm-pack and Python consumers are important because checkout imports can hide missing files, undeclared sibling dependencies or broken exports.

I would then separate evidence layers. Pure codec tests prove parsing and contracts; real PostgreSQL races prove selected lock and replay behavior; actual process and socket tests prove ownership; browser media tests prove selected playback observations; provider runs prove selected real inference. None automatically closes the other layer. Current documentation marks selected I01-I21 capabilities and later receiver/origin prerequisites qualified, while I22 and all seventeen complete P2 charter rows remain planned. The latest audit records remaining lifecycle findings and rare timing flakes. A strong interview answer explains those gaps and proposes the next measurable gate instead of relabelling the whole project production-ready.

followups.question: What would you simplify for a first-time SDK user?
followups.answer: Offer a small opinionated composition example with explicit authority selection, one accepted-input path and one recovery walkthrough, while retaining narrow public ports underneath. The starter already demonstrates that direction. Do not hide scope, unknown outcomes or cleanup behind magical defaults merely to shorten the example.

followups.question: What would you improve next?
followups.answer: First close the known stop/End lifecycle gaps with held-input and fresh-process recovery assertions. Then complete the missing I22 release scenario. Qualified prerequisites are not the complete gate: README/Design call it Planned while the charter calls it Partial; all seventeen complete acceptance rows remain Planned.

chapter_title: P2 One conversation across channels
title: Defend the unresolved lifecycle findings
question: If an interviewer points to the latest audit, which P2 or joined lifecycle limitations would you discuss first?
answer: I would start with the two high-priority joined findings rather than claim the local demo has complete shutdown safety. GW-A1 records that a normal stop can exhaust pending input attempts while the Parent endpoints are already closing and the gateway still claims work. GW-A2, with medium confidence, records that End can strand a room's final input because the worker stops before the binding is closed and revoked. These are composition and lifecycle-order problems, even though the individual SDK has explicit ownership and recovery mechanisms.

The repair direction is to stop new dispatch admission while dependencies still exist, drain or truthfully retain accepted in-flight work, observe dependent closure, then close the shared sources. Validate this with actual barriers and processes: accept the last input, pause at preparation or possible-call boundaries, trigger End or normal stop, then restart and reconcile the original identity without spending attempts on a closed dependency. Also inspect the inverted shutdown budgets, interrupted scripted playout that may repeat speech, and no_audio reported while acceptance is unresolved. Explain which are verified defects and which need further lifecycle proof. Do not describe these proposed fixes as already implemented.

followups.question: What evidence would close the recorded GW-A2 concern?
followups.answer: Accept the final room input, hold processing, invoke End, then restart a fresh owner. Reconcile the same receipt/operation without lost work or exhausted attempts and show later useful progress. GW-A2 is recorded with medium confidence; this controlled schedule should confirm the defect before validating its repair.

followups.question: How would you prevent retry exhaustion during shutdown?
followups.answer: First define the closing transition and which component owns it. Stop eligibility or classify shutdown before charging a fresh attempt, retain original preparation and possible-call state, and keep required endpoints alive until dependent dispatch is closed. Test actual interleavings before selecting the final mechanism.

followups.question: Would increasing every timeout fix it?
followups.answer: No. Larger budgets can reduce incidental flakes but do not establish correct dependency ordering or retained ownership. Use a coherent budget hierarchy plus observed resource closure, and preserve the primary failure when cleanup remains unresolved.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: A cheap authentication pass before SQL
question: Why does rejectForged authenticate using the signed timestamp before opening a database connection, then authenticate again inside the transaction?
answer: The first pass rejects forged bytes and malformed payloads before acquiring a PostgreSQL connection or durable admission lock. It reads the timestamp through a property descriptor, avoiding a caller getter, and passes that signed timestamp as the comparison clock. Consequently this pass checks MAC and payload integrity but deliberately cannot establish present freshness. The four-call in-memory admission check still happens before this precheck; the guarantee is specifically about avoiding SQL resource consumption.

The transaction later authenticates the original input against database time after the shared admission lock. A correctly signed but stale request can pass the cheap pass and still fail there. This two-stage ordering limits forged traffic impact without letting a caller-selected timestamp authorize new durable input. The tests distinguish zero connections for forged input from one cleanly rolled-back connection for stale signed input.

followups.question: Why not trust Date.now for the second check?
followups.answer: The selected durable admission contract uses PostgreSQL time after locks. A host clock check before a long lock wait can become stale. It can be a transport filter, but it should not replace the protected authority clock.

followups.question: Does the first pass bypass overload?
followups.answer: No. The in-memory four-call check occurs before precheck. The code promises forged requests take no SQL connection or durable lock; it does not promise authentication has priority over every local resource limit.

followups.question: Does a valid signature identify the customer?
followups.answer: It identifies the configured synthetic provider observation. The current verified sender association supplies account and conversation scope inside the durable intake path. A signed sender string alone cannot select an arbitrary customer account.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Reject complete byte overflow before parsing
question: Why does parseEventJson call text on the complete wire string before strictJson?
answer: text checks the complete string and its UTF-8 byte count before recursive parsing. This separates the wire ceiling of 32,768 bytes from the smaller semantic text ceiling. A short-looking JavaScript string can encode to more bytes, and a valid message padded with whitespace can exceed the wire limit without changing its eventual JSON value. Rejecting before parse prevents that transport envelope from bypassing the declared budget.

strictJson then retains duplicate-key evidence and bounds recursive structure before projection. Only afterward does the event-specific closed schema apply. The order matters because ordinary parsing and schema projection could discard duplicate fields or spend work on a frame that should have failed immediately. Exact-boundary tests accept a valid padded frame at the ceiling, reject one extra byte, and separately reject deep nesting. They test visible contract behavior rather than merely spying on the parser.

followups.question: Why does whitespace count if it is semantically irrelevant?
followups.answer: The transport receives every byte before semantic projection. The exact-boundary test pads one valid JSON event with whitespace: its canonical identity stays equal at 32,768 bytes, then one added byte rejects. Equal meaning does not imply equal parsing or buffering cost.

followups.question: Why not truncate to the allowed body size?
followups.answer: Truncation silently changes the accepted user request and its replay semantics. A later original replay can then appear changed or two distinct requests can collapse. Reject the whole input and let the caller submit an explicit new bounded request.

followups.question: Does a byte cap stop every parser attack?
followups.answer: No. Depth, duplicate keys, invalid Unicode, field count and schema constraints remain separate. The useful property is layered bounded validation, with each guard stating the resource or ambiguity it prevents rather than claiming one universal parser defense.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Validate time as one canonical representation
question: Why does the timestamp validator combine a fixed-format regex with a Date toISOString round trip?
answer: The regex restricts the accepted spelling to millisecond UTC timestamps with a literal Z, and the text bound prevents a valid-looking prefix with extra data. The Date round trip then rejects calendar values that match the shape but normalize to a different instant, such as an impossible day. Rejecting year zero also preserves the selected cross-language date domain.

This is representation validation, not causality or authority. Equal instants written with offsets are intentionally outside this event contract rather than normalized after acceptance. That keeps canonical byte comparisons and Python/TypeScript fixtures consistent. receivedAt and occurredAt are validated before storage, but neither determines the winner of a case revision or replaces database time for grant freshness. The shared negative fixture explicitly includes both an invalid calendar date and an offset spelling, so removing either layer would change observable acceptance.

followups.question: Why reject a correct instant with plus zero offset?
followups.answer: The wire contract deliberately admits one spelling, including literal Z and three fractional digits. An offset import adapter could normalize before creating an event; replay validation must not quietly widen that domain or compare only the resulting epoch value.

followups.question: Can occurredAt order concurrent case changes?
followups.answer: No. It is a producer observation, with clock and delivery limitations. The expected-revision case authority serializes changes. A valid canonical timestamp does not become a stronger permission or prove that one concurrent request caused current state.

followups.question: Why test this through the shared fixture?
followups.answer: A local helper test could pass while another language accepts a different date domain. The same frozen negative wire cases exercise the public decoders and require stable payload-free errors, preserving the interoperability boundary rather than only one implementation detail.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: A rolled back connection is not necessarily broken
question: Why does the transaction wrapper track committed, commitStarted and broken separately?
answer: A routine domain rejection can leave the SQL connection reusable after a clean rollback. A rollback failure means its state is unsafe, while a failed COMMIT response can be ambiguous even if a later rollback command appears to succeed. The wrapper therefore starts broken from commit uncertainty and upgrades it on rollback failure. finally releases the client with that explicit flag rather than discarding every connection on every application error.

The public error also depends on the boundary crossed. A known commit followed by a hook failure, or a write whose commit started without a known outcome, becomes AcknowledgementUnknown. AssociationRequired before commitment can remain a definite domain rejection. The final nested finally decrements active admission even if releasing the pool client raises. This combination preserves business uncertainty, pool hygiene and actual call accounting; optimizing only one of those concerns would leave the other two vulnerable.

followups.question: Why attempt rollback after an uncertain commit?
followups.answer: It is cleanup, not evidence that the earlier commit did not happen. The broken flag remains true for an uncertain commit, and the application still receives an unknown acknowledgment. Cleanup commands cannot replace original-operation reconciliation.

followups.question: Should a test inspect release true or false?
followups.answer: Yes, at this pool boundary the release disposition is the observable resource contract. Pair it with public error assertions, so a correct business code cannot hide unsafe reuse and correct disposal cannot hide a falsely definite outcome.

followups.question: What does an after-commit hook failure mean?
followups.answer: The business transaction may already be committed. Treating the hook exception as rollback would lie to the caller. Preserve the committed state and report acknowledgment uncertainty while retaining the original request and receipt path for reconciliation.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Carry quote JSON without reparsing it
question: Why are P1 quote bytes kept as an opaque ASCII string instead of JSON.parse and JSON.stringify in P2?
answer: P1 canonical quote JSON can contain integer literals outside JavaScript safe integer precision. Parsing and serializing through JavaScript numbers could change those literals even when no code intended to edit the quote. quoteBytes therefore checks a bounded ASCII object-shaped envelope while preserving every byte, and quoteDigest hashes that original string. P2 transports and binds the quote; P1 retains authority for its exact semantic validation.

The stored prompt carries that same opaque payload, revision, quote ID and digest into one exact confirmation command. No current supplier state is used to fill missing bindings. The HTTP test uses two adjacent int64 values near the signed limit and asserts the actual outgoing quoteJson remains identical. This is a case where stricter local semantic parsing would weaken the protocol unless it implemented exactly the same arbitrary-precision canonical contract as the owner.

followups.question: Does the object-shaped check prove the quote is valid?
followups.answer: No. It bounds the transport envelope and preserves bytes. P1 must validate the exact quote contract and revision atomically with commitment. A digest proves matching bytes relative to the trusted binding, not semantic correctness or consent.

followups.question: Why not store only the digest?
followups.answer: The digest identifies the approved bytes but cannot reconstruct them for exact replay. Retain the original payload and identity so the same command can be validated after an ambiguous acknowledgment without reading a new mutable quote.

followups.question: Would converting every number to a string fix it?
followups.answer: That would change the P1 canonical quote schema and approved bytes. It might be a valid future owner-defined contract, but a bridge cannot silently transform existing quotes and still claim exact original confirmation compatibility.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Reuse the stored preparation before consulting a new world
question: Why does dispatch skip case inspection and agent preparation when the claim already has a PreparedDispatch?
answer: A retained preparation fixes the accepted message, case revision, operation key and complete canonical request. Re-reading the case or regenerating an agent decision during retry could produce new semantics under the same idempotency key. The dispatcher therefore initializes prepared from claim.prepared and enters case inspection and agent preparation only when it is absent. It later looks up the original operation before deciding whether a normal dispatch may accept.

Storage independently validates owner, epoch, current source binding and equality if a preparation already exists. Thus reuse is not permission to ignore current admission; it is preservation of original command meaning. Explicit reconcile is narrower still: it requires retained preparation and performs lookup only, with absence remaining uncertain. The test observes case and agent ports are not invoked on a stored-plan retry, while a separate test proves reconcile never reserves or accepts.

followups.question: Does replay still check permission?
followups.answer: Normal dispatch rechecks the original binding and claim before another guarded accept. Reconcile is separately lookup-only and may recover a historical receipt after revocation. A frozen plan preserves meaning; it grants neither fresh permission nor exactly-once generation before that plan was persisted.

followups.question: Why can normal dispatch accept after absence but reconcile cannot?
followups.answer: They are different explicit contracts. A normal step can cross a new guarded reservation under the cooperating stable-idempotency port. Reconcile is observational; its purpose is to recover an original receipt without converting absence into new invocation permission.

followups.question: What if a known receipt arrives after the caller deadline?
followups.answer: The dispatcher retains and validates that useful durable fact before reporting the caller deadline. The late response must match the frozen operation and payload. Losing the waiter does not justify throwing away original acceptance truth.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Freeze final recognition before the first asynchronous boundary
question: Why does _voice_completed construct a new CommittedTranscript before awaiting durable acceptance?
answer: The SDK completion hook is asynchronous, while recognizer and current-turn state can advance. The function first selects the committing turn, rejects duplicate processing, and verifies an exact genuine CommittedTranscript snapshot whose input ID and body match the callback. It copies that original identity, body and recognizer request ID into frozen local data before awaiting _accept. The resulting NativeInput cannot be relabelled using a later mutable turn.

Genuine final recognition is distinct from SDK interim promotion. A delayed final keeps its original caller-bound source, and repeat commit retains one durable input and conversational context. The pinned-SDK test holds final recognition, refuses a new turn, verifies no input or generation yet, then releases it and checks the original ID. The current no_audio timeout UX can still mask unresolved acceptance; this source binding does not solve that separately recorded limitation.

followups.question: Why use an exact type check for CommittedTranscript?
followups.answer: The selected recognizer contract supplies that immutable final value. Accepting an arbitrary object with matching fields could let a different observation masquerade as genuine source finality. The type gate complements the input and body comparisons, rather than proving business consent.

followups.question: Does final recognition start generation?
followups.answer: No. The runtime durably accepts first, and the SDK hook stops automatic response continuation. Later explicit dispatch preparation owns generation from the accepted context. Recognizer finality, durable acceptance and model invocation are separately observable facts.

followups.question: What if the recognizer answers after its source closes?
followups.answer: It cannot borrow a later turn ID. The recognizer test closes A, holds its final, refuses a replacement while pending, then confirms neither A nor the next source receives a fabricated final. Cached no_audio still does not establish that a separate durable acceptance rolled back.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Stop the default SDK path after custom intake
question: Why do manual turns, text_input false, session_host false and StopResponse all appear in the native adapter?
answer: The settings address different competing consumers. Manual turn handling and disabled preemptive generation control timing; text_input false prevents room I/O from independently consuming the custom text stream; session_host false disables RemoteSession driving and observation of this session. After the custom voice hook performs durable intake, StopResponse prevents SDK default reply continuation. Manual mode alone is insufficient: the positive-control SDK test shows a normal hook still generates after commit.

The hook also retains a source handoff and schedules its release with call_soon so it unwinds through the SDK boundary before explicit preparation proceeds. That prevents custom dispatch from racing the still-active SDK turn callback and creating duplicate conversational context. The selected implementation therefore has one durable intake path and one later generation owner. These are pinned-SDK composition choices, with actual session tests; they are not a claim that LiveKit default behavior is defective.

followups.question: Why not suppress the duplicate generated answer later?
followups.answer: That is too late for a contract requiring durable intake before generation. The model may already consume resources or produce observable output. Prevent the competing invocation at the ownership seam, rather than hiding only the final text.

followups.question: Why call_soon instead of releasing immediately?
followups.answer: The retained handoff must outlive the hook body until StopResponse unwinds through the SDK callback. Immediate release could allow explicit preparation to race the SDK own turn completion. The scheduled callback preserves that sequencing contract.

followups.question: Does StopResponse cancel durable work?
followups.answer: No. It ends the SDK response continuation for this hook. Durable case cancellation has a separate authenticated command and external-effect boundary. A conversational exception cannot revoke an already accepted investigation or prove a supplier call stopped.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Read the authority clock after waiting for the binding
question: Why does NativeStore.binding acquire FOR UPDATE before its fresh clock and expiry check?
answer: A native event retains the binding ID in its original sender identity. Before new dispatch preparation or reservation, binding locks that exact native row and validates its stored shape and retained-capacity metadata. Only after those awaits does it fetch clock_timestamp and compare expiry, revocation, tenant, account, case, conversation, provider and original epoch. Time spent waiting for the row therefore consumes grant lifetime rather than extending it.

The order prevents a request from checking time while eligible, waiting behind another transaction, and then using an expired grant. It returns null for an ineligible original source so dispatch can preserve blocked versus uncertain state appropriately. The unit barrier test advances the supplied clock while the binding lock is held and asserts denial after release, then proves an independent valid binding progresses. This is a lock-ordering proof with a synthetic driver, distinct from the real PostgreSQL gate.

followups.question: Why compare account and provider fields if the binding ID matches?
followups.answer: An identifier lookup alone does not validate the retained event relationship. Corrupted or forged message fields must not borrow another binding authority. The full comparison checks the original scope and source semantics before another protected call.

followups.question: Does the lock freeze a remote carrier call?
followups.answer: No. It orders database decisions about new admission. A call already reserved outside SQL may still execute after the lock is released or the grant later expires. Preserve its original identity and uncertainty at that external boundary.

followups.question: What constitutes useful progress in the test?
followups.answer: After the expired blocked request settles, an independently valid binding must still succeed. A test that only proves every call is denied could hide a broken clock, leaked slot or universal authorization failure rather than a correct temporal fence.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Recheck disclosure after the public case read
question: Why does readNativeResult run a second protected native-grant check instead of returning its first snapshot?
answer: The first transaction derives the trusted route from the current native bearer and reads the original result. The code then releases SQL and calls the public P1 case adapter. Because the grant may expire or be revoked during that external await, a second protected transaction rereads it and compares the original binding, room, participant and complete logical reference. Only that final admission permits disclosure.

This keeps external I/O outside database transactions while preventing stale authorization from authorizing a returned result. One shared outbox call slot remains owned across the sequence, so releasing a connection does not make the whole operation unbounded. The result explicitly reports separate observation times and atomic false. A denied final check is not an unknown business write: it is a failed disclosure with no mutation. The transaction test verifies the public case read happened, the final permission failed and rollback produced no insert or update.

followups.question: Does the second check create an atomic P1 and P2 snapshot?
followups.answer: No. It validates disclosure permission at the final P2 point. The case and result remain separately timed observations. The returned atomic false flag prevents consumers from treating equal revisions or a late permission check as cross-store freshness.

followups.question: Why compare the same room and participant again?
followups.answer: A bearer-derived read must remain bound to the original principal context throughout the operation. Finding some eligible binding afterward would silently retarget the disclosure. Exact original binding and route comparisons prevent that substitution.

followups.question: Why must a denied read release its slot?
followups.answer: Otherwise one correct authorization denial could permanently consume finite capacity and block unrelated later reads. The negative case should preserve privacy, while a subsequent valid read proves that actual ownership and rollback cleanup completed.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Retain the evidence that admitted a new provider operation
question: Why store predecessor and evidence digests instead of recomputing the admission reason from the latest operation status?
answer: A new provider operation after definitive nonacceptance needs a durable reason explaining why it was allowed. admissionFor validates a retained send result or lookup observation, then records its exact predecessor operation, attempt and evidence digest. createOperation stores that immutable witness with the new operation. Later observations can change current eligibility without rewriting the serialized evidence that justified the earlier admission.

New reservations also inspect every bounded earlier operation, not only the latest one. An old operation may later disclose acceptance or conflict and veto another reservation. The temporal-history fixture deliberately creates contradictory late provider evidence after a newer operation exists: original attempt history remains identical, but another send becomes unknown and explicit retry is held for prior_operation_evidence. This distinction is essential for auditability; current truth must block unsafe future work without pretending a previously admitted operation never had a valid witness.

followups.question: Why hash the specific evidence instead of just recording its status?
followups.answer: The status alone cannot identify the observation that was actually validated at admission. A digest and exact identity bind the witness to immutable bytes, so later contradictory reports remain distinguishable rather than replacing the historical reason.

followups.question: Can late evidence invalidate the old admission receipt?
followups.answer: It can change what new work is safe now, but it must not rewrite the already committed witness or original receipt. Preserve both facts and show the conflict. A past serialized decision and present eligibility are different questions.

followups.question: Does the fixture prove a real carrier obeys the contract?
followups.answer: No. The fixture deliberately returns late acceptance after a nonacceptance witness, violating the assumed provider contract. It proves unchanged admitted history and a conservative future veto under contradiction. Production deduplication or terminal-negative fencing still needs the actual carrier’s documented behavior and qualification.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: A callback must win admission to veto a new reservation
question: Why are callback authentication, exact attempt correlation and the shared admission lock all required?
answer: CallbackStore authenticates and snapshots the raw callback before scheduling I/O, then rechecks transport freshness with database time. Replay lookup is scoped to the authenticated provider event. For a new observation, the exact original attempt, provider operation key and request digest must match before capacity or insertion. A later association or body label cannot supply another recipient relationship.

The callback write and outbound reservation share the durable admission lock. That gives a precise race result: a retained callback vetoes a new reservation, but one arriving after a call was already reserved cannot revoke that possible I/O. The callback-race fixture exercises both schedules with barriers, including a paused admitted send followed by revocation and callback. This code therefore combines authentication, immutable correlation and serialization; dropping any one allows a different class of forged, misattributed or racy evidence.

followups.question: Why authenticate a callback that appears to be a replay?
followups.answer: The event ID must not become an unauthenticated receipt oracle. Authenticate each request’s exact signed bytes, then compare its canonical observation with the retained event. Fresh signatures or reordered JSON can replay; changed semantic fields under that ID cannot.

followups.question: Can a failed callback permit resend?
followups.answer: No. The selected callback contract is evidence with a conservative new-reservation veto. A provider failure report does not automatically establish reliable nonacceptance, and it cannot grant current recipient permission or choose a replacement operation key.

followups.question: What does the retry-first schedule prove?
followups.answer: It proves the limit of the database fence. Once reservation admitted the call, later callback or route revocation cannot undo external I/O. The test must retain the original attempt and known response, rather than falsely classify cancellation before dispatch.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Idle polling should respond to progress rather than activity
question: Why exclude parked uncertain rows from automatic eligibility and reset idle backoff only after dispatch?
answer: The audit found an uncertain input with a missing sender association could be reclaimed every poll. Because it remained a possible external operation, the state could not truthfully become not_executed. Current eligibility excludes the precise parked combination uncertain plus association_required, while explicit step and lookup-only reconcile remain available. That prevents one unadvanceable row from repeatedly consuming automatic attempts and scan attention.

The gateway separately treats only dispatched status or a local nudge as a reason to reset its idle delay. Merely inspecting or reselecting a row is activity, not useful progress. A mocked dispatcher repeatedly returning uncertain now causes exponential idle backoff instead of a hot loop; a fresh local accepted input still nudges immediate work. These are two complementary choices: storage describes useful automatic candidates, and the loop avoids treating every candidate observation as success. They do not establish global fairness or fix all joined shutdown findings.

followups.question: Why not delete the parked row?
followups.answer: It may represent a possible external acceptance and retains replay protection. Removing it would trade CPU pressure for lost business truth. Parking changes automatic discovery only; retained history and explicit reconciliation remain available under their own permissions.

followups.question: Do fewer than eight steps in 400 ms prove production performance?
followups.answer: No. The test counts step calls while repeatedly returning one uncertain ID; it distinguishes backoff from a constant 20 ms loop. It does not measure production latency or fairness. Storage eligibility and the separate nudge control must also preserve useful later work.

followups.question: Could a remote input wait longer than a local one?
followups.answer: A local input can nudge the loop immediately, while externally visible eligible work may wait up to the configured idle delay. That latency tradeoff is explicit. A future notification transport could reduce it without replacing durable discovery.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Reserve capacity to record facts already learned
question: Why give carrier-result recording its own four slots instead of using the four ordinary outbox calls?
answer: A carrier response is useful truth that may arrive after the ordinary read or reservation slots are saturated. The previous shared cap could reject recordResult, leaving a known accepted_by_provider outcome permanently unknown locally. The store now tracks recording work separately: ordinary capacity is calls.size minus recordings, while recording has its own four-slot cap. Both kinds remain in the owned call set until actual settlement.

The recording helper also uses its own non-aborted signal, so caller abandonment does not discard a validated late fact. Identity and canonical-result checks still run in SQL before insertion. The change is a bounded reserved lane, not an unlimited bypass or promise to survive storage failure. The regression test holds all four normal calls, verifies another ordinary read is overloaded, then confirms an exact carrier result is inserted and unknown count remains zero.

followups.question: Why exactly four recording slots?
followups.answer: Four matches the maximum configurable outbox task count; the default is two. The recording lane is reserved structurally, not selected from a throughput benchmark. Raising the task maximum would require reviewing recording admission, shared SQL connections and retained close ownership together.

followups.question: Does this give recordings a separate database pool?
followups.answer: No. It separates application call admission while sharing the configured pool and transaction machinery. It prevents rejection at the local four-call guard; database availability, locking and connection limits remain independent constraints that can still delay or fail recording.

followups.question: Can a late response overwrite a conflicting retained result?
followups.answer: No. Recording validates the original request tuple and canonical result. Equal data replays; changed data conflicts. Reserving a lane preserves capacity for truth, not authority to replace immutable facts or accept an unrelated carrier response.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: An index migration still needs protected ownership
question: Why does the v9 owner upgrade explicitly lock indexed tables and revalidate before its index-only DDL?
answer: v9 adds three operating indexes and changes no business row, but it still changes the validated catalog and schema metadata. The owner first acquires the schema advisory transaction lock, checks the supported source version, then takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks on metadata, admission and affected tables. It revalidates the catalog after acquiring those locks before any index DDL. Quiescence remains the required operational procedure; locks protect the actual maintenance boundary.

The explicit ordering closes a race in assuming that an earlier validation remains current while waiting for DDL locks. A repeated complete v9 invocation revalidates under protection without recreating indexes or downgrading state. The synthetic ordering test asserts lock then validate then DDL, and the real populated fixture interrupts after index creation to prove rollback, compares original rows and receiver identity, then verifies the exact three indexes and unchanged legacy reads.

followups.question: Why validate again after locking?
followups.answer: An earlier check can become stale while waiting for locks. The protected revalidation ties the assumptions to the state actually being changed. Advisory locking coordinates cooperating owners; explicit table locks additionally protect the relevant maintenance state during the transition.

followups.question: Does index only mean the entire database is byte identical?
followups.answer: No. schema_metadata intentionally changes version, definition digest and catalog snapshot, and the three indexes appear. The real fixture excludes metadata when comparing business snapshots, preserves receiver identity and legacy reads, and proves the interrupted owner transaction rolls all changes back.

followups.question: Can serving code automatically repair a missing index?
followups.answer: Not under this contract. Runtime performs validation using its restricted role and reports mismatch. Schema creation, upgrade and repair remain explicit owner operations so an ordinary request or startup does not acquire hidden DDL authority.

chapter_title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
title: Do not derive the external receipt from source UUIDs
question: Why does the operation client validate operation key scope and digest, yet accept an independently returned receipt UUID?
answer: The original P2 operation UUID identifies the accepted input processing intention. The input receipt UUID identifies durable intake, and the external receipt identifies acceptance by the cooperating authority. They are separate identities. The client checks that the returned operation key, full account scope and payload digest match the original request, then validates the independent receipt UUID instead of deriving it from the P2 source IDs.

At the origin-bound application bridge the external receipt is the actual P1 work UUID; a caller correlation ID is not proof of that join. checkedPrepared retains original receipt, event, message and sender fields in canonical request bytes. A malformed or mismatched response to accept remains OutcomeUnknown, while the corresponding failed lookup is Unavailable. Neither outcome permits replacing the operation key. The loopback test returns a wrong digest first, proves those distinct errors, then returns an exact binding and demonstrates later useful acceptance.

followups.question: Why not require receiptId equals operationKey?
followups.answer: They identify different commitments. Requiring equality would impose an unstated allocation policy on the external authority and could hide fabricated receipts in tests. Validate each domain and prove the relationship using retained request correlation and the actual authority receipt.

followups.question: Why is the wrong accept response unknown rather than rejected?
followups.answer: The remote service may already have committed before returning malformed or miscorrelated bytes. The client cannot conclude nonacceptance. A read failure is unavailable because that read creates no new obligation; operation-specific reconciliation must preserve the original request.

followups.question: Can the input digest alone establish provenance?
followups.answer: It binds bytes relative to a trusted source record, but identical text can be two legitimate inputs. Origin identity needs the original operation and receipt relationship as well. A matching body digest without the retained scoped source join is insufficient.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Choose a delegation boundary
question: Why did this project build a remote specialist after implementing native LiveKit tools and tasks?
answer: The controlled baseline has two modes: a direct function tool and a tool that enters an AgentTask through TaskGroup. Both use the same PolicyInput in a real AgentSession with a scripted model, hold evaluation at a barrier, answer a separate read-only question, then observe the eventual result. Its test compares equal results and fingerprints, one completed evaluation and zero active work after cleanup. This establishes native orchestration behavior, not model quality or process recovery.

The remote specialist introduces Python-to-TypeScript contracts, independent resource limits and a separately authenticated deployment boundary. P1 supplies durable acceptance, issued attempts and result recording; the HTTP service performs one bounded read-only calculation. Remote execution is justified by isolation and a real consumer boundary, rather than by assuming another process improves latency. It also costs serialization, authentication, network uncertainty, resource ownership and more complicated cleanup.

In an interview, defend both choices. A small local conversational subtask should usually remain a native tool or task. Work that must survive the conversational process needs durable authority, irrespective of whether the computation is local or remote. The final fair three-way performance and quality comparison remains separate release work; the baseline alone does not establish that remote delegation wins.

followups.question: Would TaskGroup recover after a worker process dies?
followups.answer: The baseline does not provide that guarantee. Its tasks belong to one SDK session and process. Recovery must inspect persisted accepted work and issued attempts through P1, retain the original logical identity, and request a genuinely new eligible issuance when required.

followups.question: What would make you remove the specialist service?
followups.answer: If all consumers are Python, isolation brings little operational value, and measurements show transport overhead dominates useful work, I would keep the same typed execution and evidence contracts behind a local adapter. Durable acceptance and exact action authorization would remain separate.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Keep one execution authority
question: Which state does P3 own, and why is the specialist HTTP registry not another accepted-work queue?
answer: P1 owns immutable accepted work, execution issuance, result disposition, delivery intent and guarded action receipts. The P3 coordinator composes public ports and stores no competing accepted-work ledger. Its durable input is the canonical request body submitted through P1's work API. P3 projection, processing and refresh stores contain derived references and observations over that authority.

The specialist's AttemptBoundary is a finite live permit map. It authenticates a principal, validates scope and evidence, rejects a conflicting active attempt, and reserves global and per-principal capacity. Release requires the actual minted permit object. It has no timer that deletes active work, no retry scheduler and no recovery ownership. A server restart loses those ephemeral observations without changing whether P1 accepted or issued the work.

Consider a server restart after P1 issues work. The specialist loses its live permit map; P1 still retains the accepted request and issued attempt. Finding no HTTP status therefore cannot authorize another call. Recovery must use the original P1 command and issuance rules. A broker notification could wake that reconciliation, but it cannot become another decision maker about retries. Likewise, status=running and durable=false describe a live computation, not a durable business receipt.

followups.question: Could Redis or NATS own the retry queue instead?
followups.answer: That would require an explicit authority redesign, including atomic acceptance, identity retention and reconciliation with P1. Adding a broker notification is easier: P1 remains authoritative and workers reconcile by original work identity when a notification is duplicated or lost.

followups.question: Why retain permits until explicit release?
followups.answer: A deadline can stop the caller while computation still uses CPU, memory or a provider request. Releasing the slot at waiter timeout would admit replacement work before the original settled and make the configured concurrency bound fictional.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Design a cross-language contract
question: What must Python and TypeScript agree on beyond a JSON schema?
answer: They must agree on exact supported fields, primitive types, bounds, version handling, canonical encoding and semantic identity. P3 bounds requests to 16 KiB and results to 8 KiB, with finite node count, nesting depth and a maximum 60-second request window. Its Python integer validator explicitly rejects booleans even though bool subclasses int. Equivalent TypeScript checks must reject unsafe or nonintegral numbers.

A request binds tenant/account scope, delegation identity, case, request revision, context/evidence references, result route and deadline. Attempt correlation is separate from the immutable logical fingerprint, so a new authorized attempt does not silently change accepted business input. Receiving code reparses even caller-created frozen dataclasses; a typed value is not evidence that it passed the boundary correctly.

Shared valid and invalid fixtures exercise the actual producer/consumer boundary, including unsupported versions, changed identities and schema-valid but unsupported facts. The current facades explicitly separate original v1 policy, fixed-policy v2 and origin-bound v3 envelopes. That costs more API surface, but prevents a new schema from silently changing the meaning of an old consumer. A schema library alone cannot establish factual support or permission to act.

followups.question: Why reject unknown fields rather than ignore them?
followups.answer: Suppose a producer adds an approval flag while an old consumer ignores it: the producer and consumer can disagree about the same command. These envelopes reject extra fields instead. To add behavior, define a supported version and prove producer/consumer compatibility; passing JSON syntax is insufficient.

followups.question: Does a matching SHA-256 prove the result is correct?
followups.answer: It proves byte identity relative to the digest, assuming the digest came from a trusted binding. It does not establish that the input was authorized, the computation was correct or the result applies to the current case. Those checks remain separate.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Authenticate service scope
question: How do you stop a specialist caller from choosing another tenant in the request body?
answer: The request body carries scope for correlation, but authority comes from trusted construction of LocalTrust and its configured PrincipalGrant records. Authentication hashes the bearer token and compares equal-sized digests with constant-time comparison across a bounded grant inventory. Authorization then checks the authenticated principal's allowed scope and the specific invoke, result, cancel or evidence capability.

Evidence access is separate: the caller must have permission for the selected source ID, and the registry resolves only configured immutable records. The HTTP invoke path requires result permission as well as invocation and evidence permission. The coordinator and runner also verify that their injected P1 clients expose the expected configured WorkScope before durable operations. A model-generated tenant label or a matching correlation ID cannot bypass those construction-time bindings.

The current local trust mechanism is intentionally finite and synthetic; it is not enterprise identity infrastructure. The latest audit also records a narrower remaining issue: status and cancel permissions are scope/capability checked but are not bound to the principal that originally started the attempt. State that limitation clearly and propose an explicit starting-principal binding if independent same-scope principals require stronger isolation.

followups.question: Why separate result and invoke grants?
followups.answer: The invoke endpoint needs invoke, result and evidence grants because it returns output from selected sources in the same exchange. A status endpoint needs result permission, and cancellation needs cancel permission. The held-socket test rejects mismatched grants; these capability checks do not currently bind status/cancel to the starting principal.

followups.question: How would you fix the same-scope principal gap?
followups.answer: Retain the authenticated starting principal with the exact active attempt and require the same identity for status/cancel unless an explicit administrative delegation grant permits otherwise. Add two-principal same-scope tests, preserving independent operation permissions and safe unknown-attempt diagnostics.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Persist before acknowledging delegation
question: Walk through a coordinator submission and its lost-acknowledgement behavior.
answer: The coordinator snapshots and runtime-validates the request before its first await. It first looks up the original idempotency key. If work already exists, it validates the persisted canonical bytes and compares the appropriate logical semantics before returning the retained record. For new work it reads the trusted case adapter, checks exact scope/case/revision and cancellation, checks the finite deadline window, and submits the entire canonical envelope through the public P1 work API.

The important failure cut is a possible commit followed by acknowledgement loss. The coordinator performs one lookup by the original delegation key; it does not submit a second proposal, replace the deadline, or guess that the write failed. If the original record is found, it returns that validated winner with created=false. If the read is absent or unavailable, acknowledgement_unknown remains the honest result.

The case read is an admission preflight rather than an atomic action guarantee. A later case revision can make accepted read-only work outdated; exact action commitment still rechecks case authority. This design preserves useful historical computation while preventing acceptance from being mistaken for permission to mutate the booking.

followups.question: Why look up replay before checking the current case?
followups.answer: An already accepted command must remain readable and replayable after the case changes, cancellation or deadline expiry. Revalidating new-admission conditions first would hide original truth or accidentally encourage a caller to create a replacement command.

followups.question: What if two callers both miss the initial lookup?
followups.answer: Both callers may legitimately reach submit after missing the first read. P1 must choose one retained record. The coordinator then validates that winner; the schema3 accept test shows two submit attempts but one record and one created=true response. That fake-port test checks reconciliation logic; independent-process durability requires the separate PostgreSQL gate.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Separate acceptance from invocation
question: Why does only Issuance.created=true permit a specialist call?
answer: Acceptance means P1 durably retained a bounded request. Invocation needs a distinct P1-issued attempt with an owner, command identity, epoch and lease. The runner observes current work, returns an already eligible result without reinvocation, and asks the public execution port to issue the caller's explicit command. Only a newly created issuance can proceed toward HTTP.

An existing issuance may already have reached the specialist, so a replayed command is observation only. An ambiguous issue acknowledgement is reconciled by find_issue; even if it finds the grant, this runner does not invoke. Before a new invocation, the runner performs another exact observation and requires running status, no cancellation, the same current attempt/owner/epoch and an unexpired grant. It creates wire attempt correlation deterministically from the issued UUID while preserving the accepted logical fingerprint.

There are two different crash windows. A crash after issuance but before HTTP can leave an unused grant; replay still cannot invoke because the caller cannot prove that window. A cancellation after the fresh read can also race with transport admission: the read does not fence HTTP. P1 determines the result disposition at completion, and any later action needs its own atomic guard. Another invocation requires an explicit new command that P1 actually creates when eligible.

followups.question: Why not invoke after finding an ambiguously issued grant?
followups.answer: Finding a grant proves issuance, not whether the original caller sent HTTP. Reinvocation could duplicate an already-running computation. The current contract makes replay lookup-only and requires an explicit fresh eligible issuance for another invocation.

followups.question: Does the HTTP server independently verify the P1 grant?
followups.answer: In this wire version it authenticates its own local service principal and validates the bounded attempt contract. It does not independently query P1 issuance. The issued-execution guarantee belongs to the trusted runner path, not arbitrary direct HTTP callers.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Bound the entire HTTP lifecycle
question: Where are the resource limits, and why is a semaphore around model invocation insufficient?
answer: The TypeScript service separately caps connections, in-flight requests, active invocations, per-principal invocations, header bytes/fields, header time, body time, invoke time, response time and close time. Defaults include sixteen connections/requests, four active attempts and two per principal; these are configured ceilings rather than measured production capacity. The bounded parser admits only explicit POST endpoints and validates framing before capability handling.

An invocation semaphore alone leaves slow headers, oversized bodies, response backpressure, open sockets, decoding and cleanup unbounded. P3 reserves and observes each relevant lifetime, translates failures to fixed safe codes and starts no listener merely because a module is imported. The document capability adds its own finite workers and provider ownership inside the same authenticated transport boundary.

On timeout, disconnect or close, the server asks cooperative work to abort while retaining ownership until evaluation settles. This is essential for a real capacity bound: returning a 504 cannot free memory or provider work that still runs. A production extension would measure each layer under adversarial slow peers and declare admission behavior under saturation instead of treating these small local defaults as a scale benchmark.

followups.question: Why cap requests separately from connections?
followups.answer: Connection and request lifetimes differ, and a request may retain body, handler or response resources even when invocation never starts. Independent bounds make the maximum outstanding parser and application state explicit rather than relying on one downstream semaphore.

followups.question: What should happen at capacity?
followups.answer: The socket test holds one noncooperating evaluation past its deadline: the client gets deadline_exceeded, active remains one, a replacement request gets capacity and close reports cleanup_incomplete. Only releasing the held evaluator frees admission. This proves that configured bounds follow actual ownership rather than the first returned timeout.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Cancellation stops a waiter first
question: What happens when the LiveKit SDK cancels a tool that is waiting for delegated work?
answer: P3 treats waiter cancellation, business cancellation and remote cooperation as separate events. The coordinator creates an owned task and shields it from cancellation of the external waiter. A timed-out write returns acknowledgement_unknown; a timed-out preflight returns a deadline error and marks abandonment so it cannot start a later write. Actual I/O retains its slot until its done callback observes settlement.

NativePolicyApplication follows the same principle. After durable acceptance it owns one runner task, publishes pending progress and shields the actual run. SDK cancellation changes tool_waiter to stopped_waiting without cancelling accepted work or freeing its occupied run slot. Repeated calls inspect the original configured identity. A separate explicit coordinator cancel command records business cancellation through P1; a remote cancel response is only an observation about cooperation.

The cancellation test first waits until the specialist has actually entered, then cancels the SDK waiter. It asserts one owned run, one pending runner operation, no business cancellation and no replacement evaluation; after release the original result remains inspectable with only one issuance. This proves the post-admission case. Cancellation before a submission acknowledgement has a different uncertainty boundary and must be reconciled through the original identity; it is not proof that a background run was started.

followups.question: Why not let asyncio cancellation propagate everywhere?
followups.answer: It should propagate to the caller, but cancellation of the caller cannot undo a database commit or prove a thread or remote request stopped. Owned external operations require a retained observer, and preflight abandonment checks prevent starting new authority-changing work after the caller leaves.

followups.question: What should the user hear after interruption?
followups.answer: A truthful statement that the agent stopped waiting or speaking, with the original work still pending or unknown when applicable. The interface can inspect or explicitly request business cancellation; interruption itself should not be reported as cancellation success.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Separate the clocks and deadlines
question: How would you explain the project's deadline model under clock skew and late network responses?
answer: There are several clocks with different jobs. Event-loop monotonic deadlines bound local waits and cleanup. Wire epoch deadlines bind the accepted request's business horizon. P1 evaluates issuance/result eligibility with its authoritative database-time and lease/cancellation state. Producer completed_at metadata is correlation and provenance; it cannot overrule P1's eligibility decision.

The runner rechecks the current issued grant before starting HTTP and sends the original request deadline. Once computation starts, it may return after expiry, cancellation or supersession. A structurally and factually valid late result can still be recorded as history with an ineligible disposition. An eligible result already committed remains a historical fact after the old grant lease later expires; applicability and new delivery/action permission are evaluated separately.

The actual deadline schedule supplies a response whose completed_at_ms precedes the request deadline, then holds it until the stored recorded_at_ms is past that deadline. The asserted disposition is expired, and action is denied. A different case records eligible_at_commit, waits beyond the old lease and still observes candidate until cancellation. Those two cuts show why producer time, authority commit time and later inspection must not be substituted for one another.

followups.question: The specialist says it completed before the deadline. Can we use it?
followups.answer: That timestamp is insufficient. Validate the result and inspect its P1 commit disposition, current work/case applicability and the permission for the intended next operation. A producer can be skewed or untrusted, and network delay may place the commit outside authority eligibility.

followups.question: Does lease expiry delete a result?
followups.answer: No. Lease expiry limits an attempt owner and may affect a new completion disposition. It does not erase a previously recorded eligible result or original receipt. Later action or delivery still needs its own fresh admission checks.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Truth and applicability are different
question: A result is valid and says the customer is eligible. Why might it still be unusable?
answer: A result can be valid for its immutable request while no longer applying to the current case. The runner first validates scope, request/result correlation, canonical bytes and factual evidence. P1 separately records whether the result was eligible_at_commit with respect to execution time, lease and cancellation. Neither check means the customer's current request still matches that result.

The read view therefore derives applicability. It distinguishes missing, candidate, clarification, outdated, case_cancelled, expired, execution_ineligible and unavailable. It reads the public case adapter separately and compares the observed request revision to the immutable request revision. If the case read is foreign, malformed or unavailable, it returns unavailable without inventing current authority. The answer remains an explicitly timed observation rather than an atomic snapshot spanning every authority.

The held-run test revises the case before releasing the specialist. It observes eligible=true in the result and eligible_at_commit in P1, yet applicability=outdated. That is not a contradiction: the retained answer describes request A while the public case now describes B. A separate test makes the case reader fail and obtains unavailable rather than candidate. Neither read view commits an action, and current B needs its own work and exact confirmation.

followups.question: Can a cached green candidate badge authorize an action?
followups.answer: No. It is derived as-of metadata and may become stale without a new result-feed event. The final action boundary must atomically revalidate current case revision, exact human confirmation and the applicable work/result conditions.

followups.question: How do you explain unavailable versus invalid?
followups.answer: Unavailable means a dependency prevented establishing a fact now. Invalid means the received identity, schema or evidence demonstrably violates the contract. Treating a transient read failure as corrupt source state can block useful later processing and mislead operators.

chapter_title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
title: Verify facts after parsing
question: How does fixed-policy v2 catch a schema-valid but factually wrong specialist response?
answer: The fixed-policy verifier loads the exact scoped policy and fact records named by the accepted request. Each reference carries source identity, version, digest, media type and byte length. It rejects duplicate or mismatched source records, validates the fixed policy version/rule/threshold, and reconstructs the expected fact witnesses from the immutable facts document.

It then compares the response's rule and fact references to those expected values and recomputes the answer. The current synthetic rule is a minimum seven days' notice. No observations means missing uncertainty; distinct conflicting observed values mean conflicting uncertainty; one supported value means an eligible boolean determined by the fixed threshold. A response with plausible citations but the wrong boolean is unsupported_facts rather than a trusted result.

The observed-client test advances its local clock only after transport begins. A late, supported true result returns expired; the same delayed body with eligible changed to false is rejected as invalid_response. This proves the ordering at that Python boundary. The TypeScript fixed-policy verifier also finishes factual comparison before returning timeliness. The guarantee concerns these bounded synthetic records, not arbitrary cited prose or real-world truth.

followups.question: Why verify an already expired response?
