followups.answer: Otherwise caller mutation could change the proposal between preflight, submit and returned-byte comparison. Canonical reparse fixes the accepted meaning before concurrency begins. Frozen outer types alone do not protect arbitrary nested mutable objects supplied by callers.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Publish ownership before starting the task
question: Why reserve a publication Future before calling _spawn, and complete it in finally?
answer: With an eager task factory, _run can start and reenter read/close before create_task returns its Task. The producer therefore publishes _scan_publication first. A close observer can wait for this transfer instead of mistaking a not-yet-assigned _scan reference for no owner. The finally resolves the transfer on both success and failure; _spawn closes an unscheduled coroutine separately.

The finally resolves the barrier for both successful creation and failed scheduling. _spawn separately closes an unscheduled coroutine. This is a local handoff protocol, not a durable work receipt. The implementation comment documents the eager-task concern; the tests drive that exact reentrancy rather than depending on the ordinary scheduler to expose it. A future refactor must preserve the reservation, publication and rollback as one lifecycle.

followups.question: Why is a boolean busy flag insufficient?
followups.answer: A flag can reject admission, but close also needs a completion event for the ownership transfer. The Future tells it when the Task reference or creation failure is published so it can observe the right object.

followups.question: Does this make the operation durable?
followups.answer: No. The barrier exists only inside one event loop. Durable accepted work remains in P1; process recovery still uses the original persisted identity rather than this Future.

followups.question: Why finally rather than the success branch?
followups.answer: If creation fails, a close observer must not wait forever for an event that only success would signal. Finally completes the publication phase while the failure path preserves correct ownership cleanup.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Abandon the scan only after the last waiter leaves
question: Why does _abandoned become true only when the departing observer is the last waiter?
answer: Readers can join one published scan, with shield protecting it from an individual waiter's cancellation. At the exception branch, _waiters still includes the departing reader, so == 1 means the last observer is leaving. Only then is the scan marked abandoned. Actual reads remain owned until settlement; a fresh reader can receive a capacity error while that abandoned work drains.

When the last observer leaves, the scan is marked abandoned so its subsequent stages cannot start fresh reads as though a user were still waiting. Actual in-flight work remains owned until settlement, so a new read may still receive capacity. This deliberately separates interest in the result from ownership of the work. The returned error is also an observer outcome, not a business cancellation command.

followups.question: Why test _waiters == 1 before decrement?
followups.answer: At the exception branch the departing reader is still included. A value of one means it is the final observer. Moving the decrement earlier changes the condition and can introduce an off-by-one cancellation bug.

followups.question: Can the second reader get a full fresh budget?
followups.answer: It has its own observer timeout when it joins. That does not renew the scan business applicability or restart its work. Request waiting budgets and result deadlines remain distinct.

followups.question: Why refuse a new read after all waiters leave?
followups.answer: The abandoned scan or inspection can still use resources. Releasing its slot on observer abandonment would violate the actual capacity bound even though no caller wants its answer.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Expiry after a successful read
question: Why check the selected result deadline again after inspection cleanup?
answer: Inspection cleanup can block after a result was selected as current. The final branch rechecks the original request deadline using time.time_ns() on this process and changes only the returned observation to not_applicable when now >= deadline. This closes the tested cleanup-delay window; it is not a new PostgreSQL eligibility transaction, clock-jump immunity or a supplier fence.

The final branch replaces only the outward applicability observation with not_applicable. It does not delete the retained result or undo known delivery evidence. The selected deadline belongs to the original request; the implementation does not manufacture a new deadline from the caller timeout. This is a final local disclosure observation, not an atomic cross-store fence and not a guarantee about when the user will eventually read already transmitted bytes.

followups.question: Which clock and deadline does this check use?
followups.answer: The process wall clock in UTC milliseconds is compared with the original request deadline. It does not grant a fresh per-read duration or replace database-time authority checks. Host clock assumptions remain a limit of this local disclosure observation.

followups.question: Is this business cancellation?
followups.answer: No. The producer suppresses a current display body. It neither requests cancellation of P1 work nor claims the specialist or supplier stopped.

followups.question: Can it expire after this check?
followups.answer: Yes. The response is as of a particular check and bytes take time to transmit. The claim must state that observation boundary rather than promise permanent future applicability.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Pacing without a shadow queue
question: Why reread every discovered item even when a prior run is paced?
answer: Each bounded scan rereads prepared/source and stored work before consulting _reruns. That in-memory map only paces a later local start; it is not a done ledger or ACK cursor. Existing owned jobs and the two-job cap are checked separately. On restart, pacing can disappear and reads can repeat, while only a new P1 issuance may authorize an invocation.

This lets the process reduce repeated startup work without replacing durable P1 authority. A restart can lose advisory pacing and legitimately inspect again; only a new P1 issuance can authorize a new invocation. The full page scan and rotating admission priority also let later work progress. This is not production-wide retry scheduling, and the latest audit still records separate scan-loop failure backoff and shared-startup contention gaps.

followups.question: Does losing pacing on restart duplicate an effect?
followups.answer: Pacing is not the effect guard. The runner must ask P1 for execution permission under original identity, and replayed issuance cannot invoke. Loss of this advisory map may add reads but must not create authority.

followups.question: Why record dispatched work in a set?
followups.answer: It bounds retained pacing metadata to the currently discovered dispatched window. Pruning advisory entries does not delete source identities or acknowledge the business work.

followups.question: Could one long-running job occupy every slot?
followups.answer: It should occupy its actual owned slot through closure. Fairness and admission for other slots are separate, and unresolved close must not be hidden by pretending the job completed.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Preserve a decoded acknowledgment
question: Why decode a complete response before attempting writer cleanup?
answer: A complete, valid decoded response can establish a receipt before socket cleanup finishes. _perform preserves that value when an ordinary close Exception occurs, records cleanup_incomplete and retains the writer/slot. Malformed-response errors likewise stay primary. This does not authorize resending or make all BaseException/cancellation paths successful; the actual owner and outcome observation remain separate.

The distinction is visible in the tests: the successful decoded receipt is returned, succeeded increments, and one pending owner remains until explicit close is retried. Conversely, malformed bytes retain their primary failure even if close also fails. The decoder is a trusted synchronous boundary with its own validation restrictions; arbitrary async user work is not allowed to hide inside response decoding.

followups.question: Is successful decoding enough to free the slot?
followups.answer: No. The writer can still be owned. Outcome truth and resource truth are independent, so pending_count may remain nonzero after a successful decoded operation.

followups.question: Why require a pure synchronous decoder?
followups.answer: Purity and bounded CPU cost are trusted caller obligations. FunctionType and code flags exclude coroutine and async-generator functions, but cannot prove purity or stop an ordinary function returning an awaitable. The wrapper must honor the narrower decoder contract.

followups.question: Can cleanup failure justify a fresh command?
followups.answer: Not by itself. If the receipt is known, preserve it. If the outcome is unknown, use the original operation reconciliation contract rather than inventing a replacement identity.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Recognize a reset as observed closure
question: Why catch OSError from wait_closed but preserve other close failures?
answer: For this asyncio stream close waiter, connection_lost can leave a terminal transport OSError that is re-raised on every await even after closure. close_writer handles that family so a reset need not wedge a slot forever. Other close-observation errors remain failures with retained ownership. This is a specific adapter rule, not proof that any OSError means a remote action failed.

It does not catch every Exception. A different failed close observer can still mean closure was not established under the adapter contract, so the owner remains retained and a later explicit close retries observation. That narrow distinction fixed permanent slot exhaustion after peer resets without converting arbitrary cleanup faults into success. The code comment documents this mechanism; the socket test verifies useful calls after reset rather than only asserting an exception was swallowed.

followups.question: Does OSError prove the remote action failed?
followups.answer: No. It describes the observed transport closure. The peer may have accepted the request before resetting; operation result reconciliation still follows its original identity.

followups.question: What should diagnostics contain?
followups.answer: A finite safe error code and bounded counters. Private peer error text is not needed to preserve the distinction between unavailable transport and incomplete cleanup.

followups.question: Why test a useful call afterward?
followups.answer: A test that merely expects unavailable can pass while every slot is leaked. Later useful discovery demonstrates the negative path did not destroy reusable capacity.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: One user intention through double click
question: Why keep #textInputId until durable acceptance rather than mint on each Send?
answer: A resolved sendText call is earlier than the separate durable-acceptance observation. Retaining #textInputId lets repeated Send refer to one intention; Retry reuses the unknown input's frozen body and ID. The UI test uses a mocked port to prove equal inputs and one displayed user row, then a new ID after acceptance. Backend idempotency/conflict checks provide the independent durable boundary.

The controller deduplicates the displayed user row by input identity, while the backend remains responsible for durable idempotency and changed-payload conflicts. Disabling the button improves interaction but is not the safety authority. A later accepted input can clear the pending identity and allow a genuinely new request. The test drives repeated programmatic sends to avoid relying solely on a disabled DOM control.

followups.question: Why not deduplicate by text hash?
followups.answer: Two identical questions can be intentional at different times, and the same intention can be retried. A user-operation identity distinguishes those cases; the digest only binds bytes to that identity.

followups.question: What if the user edits while unresolved?
followups.answer: Do not silently change the bytes under the old key. The product needs a visible choice to retry the original or create a separately identified intention when the existing contract permits it.

followups.question: Does sendText resolving clear the ID?
followups.answer: It should not imply durable acceptance. The accepted acknowledgment is the separate observation that resolves the retained input under this controller contract.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Do not fall back to an older green answer
question: Why does the newest recorded but unusable result return no_delivery or not_applicable instead of continuing to an older result?
answer: The bounded current-view scan examines retained inputs newest first. A pending input with no result may be skipped. Once a recorded result is selected, however, inapplicability or absent delivery stops the search. Falling back to an older usable result would hide that newer recorded state. The old result stays retained; it is simply withheld from this current-result view.

The code distinguishes not-yet-recorded from recorded-but-unusable. It preserves old facts in storage while refusing the misleading fallback. After the potentially delayed native read, it also rechecks execution and delivery identity before disclosure. This is a scoped selection policy, not a complete global ordering guarantee across arbitrary sources or a permission to apply the displayed result.

followups.question: Can a newer pending input hide every old result?
followups.answer: The implemented policy skips a not-yet-recorded result so earlier useful truth can remain visible. It stops fallback after selecting a newer recorded result, where a different semantic boundary has been crossed.

followups.question: Does no_delivery mean no result was computed?
followups.answer: No. It describes missing delivery evidence for the selected result. Execution result truth, delivery and display applicability are separate observations.

followups.question: Is discovery order business authority?
followups.answer: No. It is part of this bounded current-view selection. The original case revision, accepted work and public guards still control business applicability and action.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Own media before publication awaits
question: Why assign the source to #fixture before awaiting publishTrack and check admitted again?
answer: The source factory or publishTrack can settle after the observer times out or End begins. Assigning #fixture immediately adopts the returned source before another await. If admission ended, stop/close it; if publication is pending, the retained reference lets timeout stop the track. Check admission again after publish so a late ACK cannot revive an obsolete room operation.

If publication itself stalls, the retained #fixture lets timeout or shutdown stop the track. The post-publication check prevents a late acknowledgment from reviving the expired operation. The five-second observer budget includes source acquisition in this path; that is a concrete limitation for user-controlled permission delays, not proof that a physical microphone was captured. The checked test uses a late fixture factory and establishes lifetime behavior rather than hardware qualification.

followups.question: Why stop the track before await close?
followups.answer: Stopping reduces ongoing capture or media production immediately. The asynchronous close still needs observation for remaining source resources; neither operation substitutes for the other.

followups.question: Why check after publish as well?
followups.answer: Admission can change during that await. An acknowledgment from an old lifecycle cannot make the room ready again or imply the user still wants to send audio.

followups.question: Does this test prove microphone capture?
followups.answer: No. It tests the source ownership contract with a controlled fixture. Physical permission, capture quality and actual returned audio require their separately scoped browser or media evidence.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Propagate the actual call budget
question: Why pass the bridge timeout into ExternalOperationClient instead of leaving its default?
answer: An outer five-second bridge budget is ineffective if its inner ExternalOperationClient still cuts off at the default two seconds. Passing callTimeoutMs selects the intended per-call budget for this opt-in composition while preserving other consumers' defaults. Earlier attestation, scheduling and total observer time still matter; matching nominal timeouts is not proof of one end-to-end latency guarantee.

The joined configuration uses a five-second dispatch step and an eight-second claim lease for new profiles; the origin hosts use the matching selected budget. Those numbers coordinate layers rather than making a universal latency guarantee. The regression holds a real local accept for 2.3 seconds and verifies success when the bridge budget allows it. That test does not prove every slow operation is safe or that a timed-out mutation can be resent.

followups.question: Why keep the old default elsewhere?
followups.answer: Changing an opt-in composition should not silently change every standalone consumer. The new optional call timeout lets the joined adapter select its budget while preserving the established default contract.

followups.question: Does an eight-second lease cancel a five-second call?
followups.answer: No. Lease eligibility and a caller or network timeout are different controls. A request may still have crossed an external boundary and require original-identity reconciliation.

followups.question: Can attestation consume budget too?
followups.answer: Yes. A complete design must account for earlier validation and attestation work and total remaining time. Passing this option fixes the documented nested cap, not every possible end-to-end scheduling delay.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Two handles for one logical recognizer
question: Why does the scripted recognizer allow two stream handles?
answer: In the selected SDK lifecycle, clear_user_turn opens a replacement STT stream before the old handle finishes closing. One retained-handle slot rejects that valid overlap; two allow the active and closing generations. This is a resource-lifetime bound, not two speakers or two accepted inputs. The regression uses a genuine AgentSession with deterministic fixture recognition, not a live ASR-quality evaluation.

The resource bound counts actual retained handles, not the number of logical conversational turns. The genuine AgentSession regression clears and commits two fixture turns, checks exact recognized snapshots and observes one stable stream after replacement. It then explicitly opens two streams, rejects a third and demonstrates capacity recovery after closure. That is stronger than increasing a constant until a smoke test looks green; it explains both the required overlap and the continuing bound.

followups.question: Does two handles mean two accepted user inputs?
followups.answer: No. Resource overlap is not intake identity. The original caller-bound turn and durable operation remain singular under their separate contract.

followups.question: Why test the framework instead of just stream()?
followups.answer: The failure comes from ordering between SDK replacement and closure. A direct stream test can establish a numeric cap while completely missing that integration sequence.

followups.question: Does scripted recognition prove ASR quality?
followups.answer: No. It proves the declared fixture path and lifecycle through the genuine runtime. Live recognition quality and provider media qualification need their own evidence.

chapter_title: Code decisions in the joined application
title: Recheck at response admission
question: Why repeat the current-room check immediately before sending an already prepared response?
answer: The exchange can finish, then yield before the HTTP handler writes its prepared body. End may change the captured room state in that gap. The override repeats the local application check immediately before admitting a successful response to the base writer. It prevents the tested late start; bytes already admitted to TCP remain an earlier observation and cannot be retracted.

This prevents an old room response from starting a successful write after the local room fence has changed. The comment also states the limit: bytes already admitted to TCP are an earlier as-of observation. It is not a cross-store atomic revocation fence and cannot retract data already sent. The socket regression deliberately changes room state in an exchange-completion callback before the response handler resumes, exercising a narrower race than ending the room during the database read.

followups.question: Why check only successful responses here?
followups.answer: The protected disclosure is the successful current-result body. Failure responses follow their finite safe error contract; the code does not need to expose private result content to report closure.

followups.question: Does HTTP host close drain all P1 reads?
followups.answer: No. The host owns its calls and sockets, while the application separately owns producer and deeper public-client drainage. Closing one wrapper cannot certify every borrowed dependency is settled.

followups.question: What if the room closes after the check?
followups.answer: Bytes admitted after the local check still represent that earlier observation boundary. The design explicitly declines a claim of instantaneous global revocation or future human authorization.

chapter_title: WebRTC from first principles
title: The complete stack
question: Trace a browser voice call through the WebRTC stack. What does each layer contribute?
answer: WebRTC combines peer connections, media tracks and data channels with browser capture APIs such as getUserMedia. Your application exchanges negotiation information through signaling. ICE selects a reachable candidate pair; DTLS-SRTP protects media and SCTP over DTLS carries data channels. Here the browser and native agent connect through a LiveKit SFU, rather than directly owning each other's business state. [W1, W3]

For a whiteboard answer I draw a control path and a media path. An HTTPS or WebSocket request that successfully joins a room is control evidence. Audio must still be captured, published, forwarded, decoded and played. Keeping the two paths separate explains why a user can see captions while hearing nothing. [W1, W3]

followups.question: Where is signaling standardized?
followups.answer: The WebRTC API does not require one application signaling protocol. Applications must exchange the required negotiation information using their chosen signaling channel. LiveKit supplies that channel and its room protocol.

followups.question: Is WebRTC always browser to browser?
followups.answer: No. Servers, SFUs and native SDKs can be endpoints. The local agent is a participant that consumes and publishes media; it is not JavaScript running in the caller browser.

chapter_title: WebRTC from first principles
title: Offer answer and candidates
question: What do SDP negotiation and ICE each contribute?
answer: SDP offer/answer negotiates parameters such as codecs, media directions, ICE credentials and DTLS fingerprints. ICE gathers candidate addresses and tests candidate pairs; nomination identifies the path used. Trickle ICE sends candidates as they become available, reducing setup waiting. Successful offer/answer alone proves neither a reachable pair nor flowing audio. [W1, W2]

In a debugging interview I would ask whether negotiation completed, whether candidates were gathered and exchanged, and which pair was selected. I would also check the SDK lifecycle before adding custom negotiation code: a second independent connection owner can race the SDK. The application should observe the transport and retain business identity through reconnect rather than reconstructing work from SDP.

followups.question: Why can a private candidate be unusable?
followups.answer: It may identify an address that the other endpoint cannot route to through its network. Candidate discovery and successful connectivity are separate observations.

followups.question: What changes during an ICE restart?
followups.answer: An ICE restart uses new ICE username/password credentials and performs new connectivity checks, potentially selecting another path. It need not create a new business operation. Let the SDK own negotiation and reconcile any ambiguous application ACK under its original key.

chapter_title: WebRTC from first principles
title: STUN TURN and restrictive networks
question: How do STUN and TURN help a caller behind a firewall?
answer: STUN can reveal a server-reflexive mapped address and is used for connectivity checks. TURN allocates a relay address and forwards packets when other candidate paths are unsuitable. ICE chooses among viable candidate pairs; a TURN path can be deliberately preferred by policy. A TURN server carries real traffic and needs capacity, credentials and reachable ports. It is not an alternative signaling protocol. [W2, W4]

For this POC I would first establish the actual configured local exposure, then test a restrictive network explicitly. A passing loopback audio test does not demonstrate corporate firewall traversal. A production design would measure connection success and setup time by selected candidate type and transport, while redacting network addresses in shared diagnostics.

followups.question: Does TURN decrypt the conversation?
followups.answer: TURN relays packets; it does not inherently become the media decryption endpoint. The endpoint encryption arrangement determines who can read content. The SFU has a separate trust role.

followups.question: Would you force TCP immediately?
followups.answer: I would diagnose first and keep the supported fallback sequence. Reliable byte transport can increase delay when loss stalls later bytes; a reachable UDP path is often preferable for interactive media.

chapter_title: WebRTC from first principles
title: Transport encryption and endpoint trust
question: How are media protected, and what does end to end encryption change?
answer: DTLS-SRTP derives keys used by SRTP/SRTCP; media packets are not simply RTP inside a DTLS tunnel. Data channels instead run SCTP over DTLS. In an ordinary SFU deployment, transport encryption ends at the SFU, which forwards media to another protected connection. Additional media E2EE can keep encoded content opaque to the SFU while authorized endpoints hold its keys. [W5, W6]

A voice agent needs authorized access to audio to transcribe or reason over it. I would draw where encryption terminates, where PCM exists and which provider sees it before making a privacy claim. In this repository I would point to scoped grants and provider isolation as application protections, without claiming that the current local showcase implements an E2EE design.

followups.question: Does HTTPS encrypt the audio path?
followups.answer: HTTPS protects the HTTP connection. WebRTC media has its own negotiated protection. Both matter, but observing an HTTPS URL proves neither successful media encryption negotiation nor end to end content privacy.

followups.question: Can an agent process encrypted audio without a key?
followups.answer: A normal speech pipeline cannot transcribe ciphertext. An E2EE architecture must deliberately authorize the agent as a decrypting endpoint or introduce a different processing design.

chapter_title: WebRTC from first principles
title: Packets time and intelligibility
question: What do RTP, RTCP and the jitter buffer do for audio?
answer: RTP sequence numbers help detect loss/reordering, while timestamps express media timing in the codec's clock domain. RTCP carries related reports and feedback. A jitter buffer trades added playout delay for tolerance of variable packet arrival. Packets arriving after their useful playout time may not improve intelligibility, even though a network retransmission eventually succeeds.

I would diagnose choppy speech with packet loss, arrival variation, concealment and buffer delay together, using interval deltas rather than lifetime counters alone. The W3C statistics specification defines jitter and jitter buffer observations. An application should connect these transport observations to actual returned audio and perceived turn timing instead of treating generated TTS bytes as proof of playback. [W7]

followups.question: Why not retransmit everything?
followups.answer: Recovery that arrives after a playout deadline cannot repair what the listener already missed. Loss recovery must fit the media deadline and the codec or receiver strategy.

followups.question: How do you estimate average jitter buffer delay?
followups.answer: For one stable inbound stream, compute 1000 × delta(jitterBufferDelay) / delta(jitterBufferEmittedCount) for an interval mean in milliseconds. Delay is cumulative seconds; emitted count represents audio samples or video frames, not RTP packets. Require a positive count delta and restart after an identity/counter reset. [W7]

chapter_title: WebRTC from first principles
title: Data channels and durable messages
question: If a data channel is reliable, why does P2 need an inbox?
answer: RTCDataChannel supports ordered or unordered delivery, with reliable delivery by default or configured partial reliability. These guarantees concern a live transport association; they do not persist an application inbox across process failure or a new session. A send can succeed locally while the receiver fails before recording business acceptance. That requires a separate stable operation identity and receipt. [W6]

P2 adds the missing boundary: authenticate the source, persist the accepted message under its original identity, detect changed payload conflicts and only then drive dispatch or generation. Reliable delivery of bytes and durable acceptance of a user operation are both useful, but they answer different questions. A browser retry must reconcile the original identity rather than infer failure from disconnection.

followups.question: What should be unreliable?
followups.answer: A transient cursor or live level indicator may tolerate loss. A business request should use a protocol with durable acceptance and explicit identity even if its underlying transport is reliable.

followups.question: Does ordering solve duplicate work?
followups.answer: Ordering only sequences messages within its defined transport context. It does not deduplicate a replay from another connection or atomically bind an input to accepted work.

chapter_title: WebRTC from first principles
title: Mesh SFU and MCU
question: Why use an SFU for an agent application?
answer: In a mesh, each publisher sends to each peer. An SFU forwards selected encoded tracks; an MCU decodes, mixes or composites, and re-encodes output. LiveKit supplies the SFU and room/track APIs used by this POC. For one caller and one agent, integration and operational consistency are the main benefits; group bandwidth savings matter when many participants subscribe. [L1]

For this POC the SFU lets a browser and a native agent exchange media using supported SDKs while the application focuses on business continuity. It does not make every participant free: track count, forwarding bandwidth and receiver decode work still matter. I would discuss a multi participant room separately from the many independent one caller rooms used by a voice service.

followups.question: Is SFU cost constant per room?
followups.answer: No. Publishers, subscribers, track selections and bitrates determine forwarding work and bandwidth. Room count alone hides very different workloads.

followups.question: What about simulcast?
followups.answer: Simulcast publishes multiple encodings of the same video source; the SFU selects a suitable encoding for each subscriber. It trades publisher uplink/encode work for adaptation downstream. Scalable video coding is a related layered-encoding approach. Neither accelerates database work or supplies durable case state.

chapter_title: WebRTC from first principles
title: Diagnose with getStats
question: Which measurements would you inspect before blaming the model?
answer: Use the selected candidate-pair report to identify the path and STUN-based RTT, then follow the relevant inbound/outbound RTP reports for byte/packet deltas, loss, jitter and concealment. RTP/RTCP-derived RTT can describe a different observation; do not mix them blindly. Finally inspect subscription, decoded audio, mute/output routing and the browser audio element. Missing fields or unsupported stats are not zero-valued success. [W7]

Next I correlate that timeline with capture, STT final, durable input acceptance, LLM first token, TTS first audio, publication and browser playout observations. The repository deliberately separates those observations. If media never arrives, changing the model prompt is unlikely to fix the problem; if media is healthy but generation stalls, a network only diagnosis is incomplete.

followups.question: Why sample deltas?
followups.answer: Most counters accumulate. Bytes over an interval estimate bitrate as 8 times the byte delta divided by elapsed seconds. Use stable stream identity and reset the calculation after a counter or stream reset.

followups.question: Can stats prove the human heard the quote?
followups.answer: No. They establish scoped technical observations. Even a browser playout or energy observation does not establish human understanding or authorize a mutation.

chapter_title: Inside a LiveKit agent session
title: Core runtime objects
question: How do Room, Agent, AgentSession and an agent server differ?
answer: Room represents the realtime participants, tracks and data transport. Agent defines conversational behavior, instructions and tools. AgentSession orchestrates input, models, turns and output. An agent server accepts dispatched jobs and runs the application entrypoint. None of those names alone implies a persisted business workflow. The P1 case and accepted work have a separate durable lifecycle. [L4, L6]

The application must decide which object owns each resource and callback. Session shutdown should release session resources, while durable work remains in P1. A model handoff changes conversational control; it does not automatically transfer database lease authority. I would ground exact API usage in the pinned adapter rather than reciting a current quickstart from memory.

followups.question: Is an Agent a durable worker?
followups.answer: Not by that name alone. A conversational Agent defines behavior. Durable work execution in this repository uses explicit P1 records, grants and recovery contracts.

followups.question: Can I use LiveKit without AgentSession?
followups.answer: The server infrastructure supports programmatic participants. AgentSession is the high level orchestration surface for a voice agent, not a requirement for every media processing job. [L7]

chapter_title: Inside a LiveKit agent session
title: Dispatch and process isolation
question: How does an agent become a participant in a room?
answer: Dispatch assigns an agent job to a room; the agent server accepts it and runs your entrypoint. That code or AgentSession must then establish the participant connection and start the required I/O. The documented process-per-job lifecycle isolates session failures, but a dispatch receipt is earlier than connected tracks or application readiness. Explicit dispatch selects a registered agent name and carries validated job metadata. [L5, L7]

I would authenticate the application that requests dispatch and validate metadata before using it as a trusted binding. Room participant identity and business identity need an explicit relationship. A successful dispatch is not readiness for inference, durable input or playback. The POC waits for mode consistent readiness and retains the case independently of whether that room worker survives.

followups.question: Why explicit dispatch?
followups.answer: It makes the intended agent and launch point visible, and avoids automatically starting an unintended worker for every room. Exact routing and options should follow the selected SDK and server contract.

followups.question: Does process isolation provide crash recovery?
followups.answer: It limits the blast radius of a job crash. It does not restore application memory or reconcile an uncertain supplier call; those require durable state and an explicit recovery path.

chapter_title: Inside a LiveKit agent session
title: Trace the voice pipeline
question: What happens from a spoken request to an audible answer?
answer: For this cascaded pipeline, published user audio reaches STT, a turn boundary is chosen, the accepted input drives model generation, and TTS audio is published back for browser playout. A realtime speech-to-speech model combines some of these stages and needs a different timing breakdown. In the opt-in P2/joined path, durable input admission must precede its dispatched generation; generation and playback retain separate observations.

I would show the correlated input and operation ID at the durable boundary, then the generation identity and output evidence. Some stages overlap, so summing arbitrary component durations can double count. A business check can run in the background while the conversation gives a truthful pending response. No stage permits the model to approve the exact supplier mutation.

followups.question: Where do you measure responsiveness?
followups.answer: Choose a concrete start and finish, such as actual end of user speech to first rendered agent audio, and keep pipeline metrics as supporting breakdowns. State capture and measurement limitations. [L12]

followups.question: What if TTS succeeds but the browser is silent?
followups.answer: That is an output path failure. Inspect publication, subscription, received packets, decode and audio playback. Preserve generated output as a fact without labeling it heard.

chapter_title: Inside a LiveKit agent session
title: Turn taking and durable intake
question: Why does the native adapter use manual turns?
answer: The opt-in P2/joined adapter needs durable acceptance before dispatched generation. It disables competing default text intake and preemptive generation, uses manual turns, and retains the original caller-bound final transcript before awaiting external work. This gives one accepted input/operation identity on replay; it does not promise exactly one generation or exactly one playback.

Manual admission trades integration work and some latency for an explicit ordering boundary. It is not a claim that LiveKit defaults are defective. VAD activity, final recognition and semantic end-of-turn are different observations. Generation identities are retained separately and bounded; retries or interruptions must not manufacture a second accepted user operation. [L9]

followups.question: Is a final transcript permission to mutate?
followups.answer: No. Recognition finality establishes an input observation. The model, durable intake, exact quote consent and action commitment remain different boundaries.

followups.question: Could you enable preemptive generation later?
followups.answer: Only with a contract that keeps speculative output separate from accepted work and prevents speculative side effects. Measure the latency benefit and test changed transcripts, cancellation and repeated commit.

chapter_title: Inside a LiveKit agent session
title: Interruption without losing truth
question: What should happen when the user barges in?
answer: A true barge-in should interrupt the old conversational output promptly. Brief acknowledgments such as "okay" may instead be backchannels; LiveKit exposes turn/interruption strategies and tuning for that distinction. Stopping speech and deciding which recognized text belongs in context are conversational policies, separate from canceling an accepted business operation. [L10, L11]

The business layer must separately decide whether accepted work should continue or receive a cancellation request. Cutting off speech does not prove a supplier call stopped. The project should retain the original accepted operation, its known results and the newly recognized input. Reconnect or interruption history must represent the observed output boundary rather than asserting that the whole generated answer was heard.

followups.question: Does every okay interrupt?
followups.answer: Not necessarily; it can be backchannel feedback. Tune using representative audio and false interruption measurements, while keeping exact business confirmation outside inferred conversation semantics.

followups.question: Should barge in cancel background work?
followups.answer: That is a product decision expressed as an explicit command. Stop output first, then apply the documented cancellation boundary without erasing prior effect truth.

chapter_title: Inside a LiveKit agent session
title: Text is a full modality
question: What changes when the same agent supports SMS and text?
answer: A text turn bypasses STT and audio playout, but still needs trusted identity, ordering, durable acceptance and response delivery semantics. LiveKit text streams are live transport, not the retained conversation store. P2 adds scoped history and dispatch; its SMS path in this POC is a signed simulation, not a production carrier integration. [L8]

SMS introduces a different sender verification and callback model. A trusted association must bind it to the correct account and case; a string in a payload cannot supply that authority. A new SMS is a distinct input even if its wording matches a voice transcript. The product should preserve channel provenance while letting the case survive all of these interactions.

followups.question: Can late joiners read old streams?
followups.answer: Do not assume realtime streams provide historical replay. The application needs retained history and a scoped read contract for a fresh session. [L8]

followups.question: Does a phone number prove the account?
followups.answer: Only the application association and verified provider path define the permitted binding. The project distinguishes retained history access from current permission needed for selected new actions.

chapter_title: Inside a LiveKit agent session
title: Reconnect and rehydrate
question: What state should survive a network drop?
answer: Let the SDK perform its supported connection recovery, while the UI reports reconnecting and fences callbacks from obsolete lifecycles. A full reconnect or fresh room can replace participants/tracks; it does not create a replacement business request. Preserve any frozen input whose ACK is unknown, reconcile that original identity, then load authorized retained history and separately timed current-case observations. [L3]

P1 work and P2 accepted inputs survive independently. Rehydration loads current permitted context using retained channel state and public case observations; it does not resubmit every visible message. I would test a disconnect after acceptance but before ACK, and a fresh room after a completed result, then verify stable original identities and no new supplier effects.

followups.question: Should the UI disable all reads?
followups.answer: It should distinguish transport health from authenticated control API availability and freshness. Safe reads may remain useful; new authority changing actions need their own admission checks.

followups.question: Can the old transcript be the new case state?
followups.answer: No. A transcript is historical evidence. The session should obtain an authorized current case view with explicit as of boundaries.

chapter_title: Inside a LiveKit agent session
title: Provider modes and observability
question: How do you know a session actually used the configured inference mode?
answer: Check the trusted selected mode, matching mint/readiness metadata, and actual correlated usage/trace observations. scripted, local_real and provider_real are distinct modes; process health or a UI badge establishes configuration only. The selected provider_real evidence does not qualify local_real, and no silent cross-mode fallback exists. Actual returned audio and checked task outcomes are still needed for the relevant media/quality claim.

For a qualified run I would inspect actual usage observations, the selected model or provider identifiers and correlated session traces, alongside the required returned audio evidence. Numeric usage supports what was invoked; it does not prove model quality. Current LiveKit observability documentation describes per component, turn and session surfaces, but exact use must match the pinned code. [L12, L13]

followups.question: Why no silent fallback?
followups.answer: It can change latency, cost, privacy and behavior while making test evidence misleading. If fallback is desired, its policy and identity must be explicit and observable.

followups.question: Does scripted testing still matter?
followups.answer: Yes. Deterministic faults can establish invariants and useful progress. Actual inference and media qualification remain separate requirements that scripted providers cannot satisfy.

chapter_title: Failure diagnosis and production recovery
title: Connected but silent
question: The room is connected and captions update, but the user hears nothing. How do you debug?
answer: First name the silent direction and one turn/track identity. For agent-to-user silence, verify response scheduling, TTS audio, the intended published track, browser subscription, advancing received/decoded audio, then permitted playback. Check mute, output routing and audio-element errors. If input audio is silent instead, begin at capture permission and track energy; healthy captions or agent output do not establish that path.

Use one correlated turn and avoid mixing counters from old tracks after reconnect. The project has separate text, SDK and browser evidence precisely because a successful earlier stage is insufficient. Preserve a useful pending or failed audio state in the UI, without marking the response heard or retrying any business effect. Transport diagnostics follow standard connection and statistics observations. [L3, W7]

followups.question: What if only the microphone direction fails?
followups.answer: Check permission and the captured track first, then local publish bytes and agent input. A working agent output path does not prove the microphone was captured or forwarded.

followups.question: Would you regenerate the answer?
followups.answer: Only after deciding the conversational retry contract. Regeneration can be useful for audio failure, but it must not repeat the accepted business operation or invent a second input.

chapter_title: Failure diagnosis and production recovery
title: Latency climbed overnight
question: How would you investigate a p95 response latency regression?
answer: Freeze the response metric, population and comparison window: for example, end-of-user-speech to first rendered agent audio, in the same mode and load. Break down endpointing, durable admission, model first output, TTS first audio and playout, allowing for overlap. Compare sample counts and tails; a changed mix of long turns or cold jobs can move p95 without slowing every stage.

In this POC I would examine event loop lag, connection establishment, read slot contention, database locks, worker startup and provider usage. The latest audit names shared startup slots and dispatch work that includes current result reads and playout, which can couple unrelated latencies. I would reproduce one constrained case, capture the timeline and change the bottleneck with an explicit invariant check. [L12, L13]

followups.question: Why not lower endpointing immediately?
followups.answer: It may reduce delay while cutting the user off. A latency fix must preserve turn quality, durable input ordering and the intended interruption behavior.

followups.question: Is sub 500 ms guaranteed?
followups.answer: No universal target follows from the JD or this repository. State a proposed SLO with a measurement boundary, percentile, load and mode, then measure it.

chapter_title: Failure diagnosis and production recovery
title: A dependency times out
question: When is retry safe and when should the outcome remain unknown?
answer: Choose recovery from the operation contract. A bounded read may retry; a receipt-bearing command replays the same original key and frozen body. A possibly dispatched mutation/send needs its exact reconciliation policy. A timeout does not prove rejection. Even a lookup miss may be inconclusive while an earlier call is paused; another invocation needs the supplier's documented stable-operation guarantees.

The repository retains possible effect markers and known results, and distinguishes ordinary ambiguous sends from an operation with an explicitly frozen idempotency capability. P1 v5 persists selected predispatch unavailable retry due times, but the current audit leaves outages after reservation outside that pacing coverage. I would present that limitation and avoid claiming one generic retry policy handles every phase.

followups.question: Does exponential backoff ensure safety?
followups.answer: It reduces pressure; it does not identify whether the previous call took effect. Stable identity, receiver or supplier semantics and current permission decide whether another call is allowed.

followups.question: Should every layer retry three times?
followups.answer: No. Nested retry policies multiply load and exceed deadlines. Give one owner the total budget and define which lower layer outcomes it may repeat.

chapter_title: Failure diagnosis and production recovery
title: Crash after a possible effect
question: The worker dies after a supplier call but before saving its result. What next?
answer: Read the original possible-effect marker and reconcile under current worker authority. A matching supplier result can establish what happened. A lookup miss alone cannot rule out an old paused request, so safe re-invocation requires the selected cooperating stable-operation contract. Without it, retain unknown and follow explicit operator recovery; do not mint another supplier key.

The recovery test should kill a real owned process at a controlled boundary, then independently inspect supplier identity and call or effect counts. Merely raising an exception before the call does not test the dangerous window. Reaping the old worker also matters: an abandoned waiter is not proof that the original process or external request stopped.

followups.question: Can the takeover issue a new supplier key?
followups.answer: That would discard the uncertainty protection. The original logical operation identity must remain fixed through reconciliation.

followups.question: What if the old worker finishes late?
followups.answer: A stale lease must fail protected writes, while known supplier truth is still reconciled under the current authority. The supplier needs its own cooperation to prevent duplicate effects.

chapter_title: Failure diagnosis and production recovery
title: Duplicate SMS and contradictory callbacks
question: A carrier retries a webhook and later sends conflicting delivery statuses. What should happen?
answer: Authenticate the callback's exact raw bytes before replay lookup. Then correlate provider scope, original attempt/key/request digest and the canonical observation. Semantically equivalent replay can retain the original receipt even when whitespace or signed transport headers differ; changed accepted observation content conflicts. A later sender association cannot rebind the old attempt or authorize another send.

Contradictory callback facts should be retained and reduced by the documented provider rule. They are evidence about the exact old attempt, not permission for a new send. A NEW reservation rechecks earlier operations, callbacks and current route or suppression under shared admission. A callback arriving after an admitted external call cannot retrospectively fence that already possible call.

followups.question: Can you just keep the latest timestamp?
followups.answer: No general contract authorizes timestamp arbitration. Provider timestamps can be delayed or conflicting, and the original immutable attempt binding is more fundamental.

followups.question: Does delivered mean acknowledged?
followups.answer: Carrier delivery evidence does not establish that the human read or understood the message. Receiver acceptance, carrier observations and human acknowledgment stay separate.

chapter_title: Failure diagnosis and production recovery
title: An old result appears current
question: The specialist says eligible after the customer changes the request. How do you prevent a stale action?
answer: Retain a factually supported result about its immutable input snapshot, but reassess applicability against the current case. An "eligible" label from a specialist is not authority. The current guarded action must validate the exact case/work/result/confirmation and commit intent with its receipt atomically. A preliminary read or refreshed badge can race a case revision and cannot replace that guard.

Before action, use the public guard that atomically checks current work and case eligibility and exact confirmation, then commits intent and its receipt. A separate preflight read is vulnerable to a race. The existing race tooling demonstrates revision first and intent first schedules; a later revision cannot silently undo a committed original intent. Semantic validity and human permission still require their own checks.

followups.question: Could a refreshed green badge authorize action?
followups.answer: No. Refresh is derived metadata from separately timed reads. Only the current guarded action transaction can decide permission at commitment.

followups.question: Should the stale result be deleted?
followups.answer: No. It remains useful historical truth and may be needed for audit and replay protection. Display pruning must preserve protected identities and unresolved processing.

chapter_title: Failure diagnosis and production recovery
title: Shutdown consumes the final input
question: How would you investigate the gateway normal stop findings?
answer: 0048 records GW-A1 as high severity: stopping Parent endpoints while dispatch still claims can exhaust input attempts. GW-A2 is also high severity, with medium confidence: stopping the worker before closing/revoking the gateway room can strand its last input. Reproduce these distinct schedules before choosing a lifecycle repair. Both remain open in the recorded snapshot.

I would draw the shutdown dependency graph: stop new admission at the right boundary, quiesce dispatch before its endpoints close, retain every admitted owner until settled, observe child closure, then close shared readers. I would prove the revised order with a final input accepted during stop and with an endpoint blocked at the write boundary, checking useful progress after restart and preserving original receipts.

followups.question: Why not suppress all close errors?
followups.answer: That can conceal unresolved owners and delete evidence too early. Preserve the primary failure and report incomplete cleanup while retaining the objects needed to observe eventual closure.

followups.question: Can a timeout justify deleting room files?
followups.answer: No. First establish that the exact owned process or group exited and was reaped. A canceled waiter alone does not establish that state.

chapter_title: Failure diagnosis and production recovery
title: Provider outage and reconnect storm
question: How do you keep one outage from overwhelming the service?
answer: Protect accepted obligations while bounding new admission, actual in-flight calls, bytes and reconnect attempts. Allocate one total retry budget only for operations that permit retry, with backoff/jitter to reduce synchronized load. Isolate expensive provider work from read/control capacity where the design supports it. Return a truthful degraded or unknown state instead of spawning unbounded replacement work.

For a production design I would isolate provider capacity from read and control paths, add fair admission and observe pending age and useful completion. In this POC, bounded slots and persisted retry pacing already illustrate part of that design, while the audit documents remaining shared pool and failure scan backoff issues. Those limits prevent me from claiming fully isolated failure domains today.

followups.question: Would you switch providers automatically?
followups.answer: Only under an explicit mode and fallback contract that preserves visibility, privacy, budget and semantic constraints. The current repository has no silent inference mode fallback.

followups.question: What do you alert on?
followups.answer: User impact: connection success, pending age, end to end response or completion SLOs, unknown effect growth and cleanup failure. Raw reconnect counts are supporting signals rather than the entire incident definition.

chapter_title: Designing for scale and durable progress
title: Scale the right subsystem
question: How would you evolve this local POC for ten thousand concurrent conversations?
answer: Define ten thousand of what: connected callers, simultaneously active audio, turns/second, or pending durable cases. Freeze call duration, active speech ratio, model mix, fan-out, bytes and retention. Measure media bandwidth, agent process capacity, inference quotas and database admission separately. More workers help only after identifying the bottleneck and checking whether downstream capacity can accept the added load.

The POC uses one local SFU and has no production-capacity qualification. The public self-hosted guide documents Redis-backed distributed room placement and a room fitting on one node. That describes many-room routing, not unlimited capacity for one room. Agent jobs and durable workers need their own scaling and failure tests; no private Cloud topology is inferred. [L2]

followups.question: What is the first load test?
followups.answer: One representative room and turn workload with a frozen manifest, then a controlled ramp. Retain raw results, queue age, errors, actual resource use and independent reconciliation.

followups.question: Why not add more workers immediately?
followups.answer: Workers can increase contention or overload a provider and database. Measure the bottleneck and retain ownership and admission invariants at each new concurrency level.

chapter_title: Designing for scale and durable progress
title: Capacity arithmetic
question: How do you estimate concurrency and backlog?
answer: For a stable measured system, Little's law relates mean work in the system L to accepted arrival rate lambda times mean residence time W. An illustrative 20 tasks/second × 3 seconds gives 60 resident tasks, including waiting work. It does not imply 60 CPU threads, a p95 bound or sufficient capacity for bursts. These numbers are an exercise, not repository results.

A dependency outage breaks steady state assumptions and grows backlog until admission or storage limits intervene. Separate active slots, pending work and retained identities. P1 and P2 preserve identity protections at capacity; evicting a display row does not create room for another protected operation. I would size retention and replay horizons as part of the design rather than just multiplying worker count.

followups.question: Why is p95 not substituted for W?
followups.answer: Little law uses averages over a stable system. Percentiles help bound user experience and burst planning, but substituting them blindly changes the calculation meaning.

followups.question: What if arrivals exceed service capacity?
followups.answer: If accepted arrivals persistently exceed completions, backlog grows until a configured bound, rejection or another failure intervenes. Set admission and retention policies deliberately. A finite worker pool alone does not bound durable backlog or retained idempotency records.

chapter_title: Designing for scale and durable progress
title: Backpressure that reaches admission
question: Where should concurrency limits live?
answer: Bound durable obligations at admission and each scarce resource at its owner: request bytes, handlers, database connections, real remote calls and retained identities. A timed-out waiter may leave the actual call running. Its slot stays occupied until the owner observes settlement. Reserve control/reconciliation capacity where needed; a per-process semaphore is not a cluster-wide or per-tenant quota.

In the joined application, ChannelPolicyExecutor limits owned jobs and retains runner ownership through closure. Shared reader capacity is reserved so background inspection cannot occupy every dispatch slot. This is a concrete useful pattern, but the latest audit still records other shared startup and read pool contention. A production extension would define tenant fairness and budget policy above these mechanism limits.

followups.question: What does the user see at capacity?
followups.answer: New durable work should receive an explicit capacity result without consuming a replacement identity. Replays and reads bypass new-work caps where their contract says so, but can still fail from unavailable I/O or a full transport pool. Expose that distinction rather than promising every read always succeeds.

followups.question: Why bound bytes as well as requests?
followups.answer: Ten small inputs and ten large images can have very different memory, CPU and downstream cost. Per request count limits alone do not constrain total resource use.

chapter_title: Designing for scale and durable progress
title: High availability without lost truth
question: How do database replication and backups affect the design?
answer: Start with the acknowledged-data failure model. An asynchronous replica can lag, so promotion may lose recent accepted commits. Synchronous replication strengthens a configured acknowledgment boundary, with latency and availability costs. Backups cover different failures and need a tested restore. Neither a live replica nor a healthy database proves that original effect keys and receipts can be recovered consistently.

This local POC uses isolated PostgreSQL and explicit migrations, not a demonstrated HA deployment. Before production promotion I would specify recovery point and recovery time objectives, test failover and restore, and reconcile committed cases, work results and external effect keys against the supplier. Losing an idempotency record while an external effect survives can be more dangerous than losing a display history row.

followups.question: Can reads go to any replica?
followups.answer: Only if the operation tolerates that freshness. Permission checks and exact commitment must use the authoritative guard; an asynchronously lagging read cannot authorize a current action.

followups.question: Why preserve tombstones?
followups.answer: A replayed old identity must not become new merely because detailed history was pruned. Tombstones or an explicit supported replay horizon protect that boundary.

chapter_title: Designing for scale and durable progress
title: Fairness and useful progress
question: How do you stop one account or one unresolved result from blocking everyone?
answer: P3 separates its discovery scan from the contiguous terminal ACK watermark, so an unresolved early event need not prevent examining later useful events. Each pass is bounded; unknown events remain unACKed. This demonstrates useful progress within the declared window, not a production tenant-fairness guarantee. Fair shares, starvation limits and control-plane reserves need separate policy and evidence.

That does not authorize skipping unknown results forever or ACKing them to free capacity. Preserve their identities and expose pending age. A production extension could apply per tenant shares and starvation detection while leaving the source authority unchanged. I would test both the negative case, where an unresolved event stays unACKed, and the positive case, where later valid work completes.

followups.question: Why separate scan and ACK cursors?
followups.answer: The scan cursor supports discovery and fairness. The contiguous watermark represents terminal processing knowledge. Advancing the latter over an unknown event would falsely assert completion.

followups.question: Can you drop old unresolved rows?
followups.answer: Display retention cannot remove protected processing identities or silently free durable capacity. Cleanup needs a separate replay and ownership contract.

chapter_title: Designing for scale and durable progress
title: Deploy while sessions are active
question: How should a rolling deployment stop taking work?
answer: Stop assigning new work before removing dependencies needed by admitted work. In the documented self-hosted media drain, active rooms continue and can accept participants while new-room joins are rejected; shutdown follows when participants leave. That has a different boundary from gateway dispatch drain or a durable worker releasing a lease. Each owner needs its own finite shutdown/recovery policy. [L2]

I would define a dependency graph and a deadline for each tier: front door, dispatch, per room workers, business runners, then shared readers. Observe actual termination before releasing a lease or deleting files. The current POC audit exposes shutdown order and budget inversions, so I would use those findings as the starting point for a tested repair rather than claim a production safe rolling deployment.

followups.question: Can SIGKILL be a normal drain?
followups.answer: It can be part of an enforced upper bound, but it leaves recovery obligations and possible external calls. A later owner must reconcile original state instead of assuming cancellation.

followups.question: Can old and new schema code overlap?
followups.answer: Only under an explicitly compatible migration and capability contract. Runtime roles must not perform opportunistic DDL while serving traffic.

chapter_title: Designing for scale and durable progress
title: SLOs for a voice and work system
question: Which objectives would you define?
answer: Define separate objectives for connection setup, usable first audio, durable input acceptance, business completion and result disclosure. Specify population, success condition, time window and exclusions. Include errors/timeouts in the user-impact accounting rather than reporting latency only for successes. A quick "still working" reply can satisfy a conversational response objective while the business-completion objective remains pending.

Then map supporting metrics to causes: event loop lag, pending age, lease takeovers, unknown effects, provider first byte time, slot saturation and cleanup incompleteness. The repository retains numeric usage and explicit observations; production alert thresholds would need measured baselines. Correlation identifiers should connect a case and its attempts while low cardinality metrics avoid unbounded labels.

followups.question: What would you page on?
followups.answer: Sustained user impact or imminent exhaustion, such as accepted work aging beyond its objective or growing unresolved effects. A single retry counter increment may be a diagnostic signal rather than a page.

followups.question: What if privacy limits transcripts?
followups.answer: Keep identifiers, timing, safe result classes and bounded structured diagnostics. Rich content should follow explicit access and retention rules rather than being copied into every metric or trace.

chapter_title: Designing for scale and durable progress
title: Multi region and a single owner
question: What changes if a business case can run in two regions?
answer: First choose the authority that orders one case's revision, exact confirmation and intent. A single writer or explicitly coordinated distributed authority must prevent conflicting commitment during partitions and failover. Place realtime rooms near users independently where supported. Replicating rows or adding regional brokers does not by itself preserve original operation identity or fence an old supplier request.

The POC has no qualified multi region business failover. I would first support region independent authenticated reads and controlled session routing, then design authority failover with original identities, database time assumptions, lease epochs and supplier reconciliation intact. Introducing a regional broker does not by itself provide a globally ordered case or external effect fence.

followups.question: Can two regions both claim on local time?
followups.answer: That risks overlapping owners if their authorities are not coordinated. The existing design uses authoritative database time after locks; a multi region design must preserve an equally explicit eligibility contract.

followups.question: Would room migration move the business case?
followups.answer: Not automatically. Media placement and case ownership have different latency and consistency requirements, so bind them deliberately rather than making room location the authority key.

chapter_title: NATS from subjects to durable consumers
title: Messaging without endpoint addresses
question: What is NATS, and how do Core NATS and JetStream differ?
answer: NATS routes publications to subject subscribers. Core NATS provides live at-most-once delivery, without an offline subscriber backlog. JetStream adds streams and tracked consumer progress; persistence across server loss depends on selected memory/file storage, replication and retention. A stream storing a message and a consumer processing it are separate acknowledgment boundaries. [N1, N2, N6]

For an original design example, I might use a live work-changed notification to wake an existing P1 poller. Losing that hint is acceptable only because durable eligibility remains discoverable. If I instead promise that a disconnected downstream audit consumer will later see every event, I need a retained event contract, storage limits and replay behavior. These are different requirements even if the messages share a subject prefix. I would first name the obligation and its owner, then select live messaging or durable consumption. Neither choice automatically makes a supplier mutation safe to retry.

followups.question: Is a successful Core publish a subscriber receipt?
followups.answer: No. It does not prove a handler processed the message or committed a business result. In an application that needs a receipt, define a response or durable read protocol with a stable original identity rather than inferring success from the publish call.

followups.question: Why not always enable durable storage?
followups.answer: Retention adds operational ownership, capacity and replay choices. Keep ephemeral hints cheap when a separate durable authority can recover missed notifications; require persistence when the messaging contract itself must bridge a consumer outage.

chapter_title: NATS from subjects to durable consumers
title: Design a subject space
question: How do subjects and wildcards work, and how would you name subjects for this application?
answer: A subject is a case-sensitive sequence of dot-separated tokens. In a subscription, * matches exactly one token and a trailing > matches one or more remaining tokens. Publish to a concrete subject. Thus continuity.eu.work.ready matches continuity.*.work.ready and continuity.eu.>, while continuity.eu does not match continuity.eu.>. Wildcards route messages; credentials/permissions authorize access. [N14]

For a hypothetical integration I would keep stable service and event concepts in the subject and put bounded correlation IDs in the validated payload. I would avoid raw phone numbers, transcripts or bearer tokens in subjects because subject names can appear in operational surfaces. A tenant token in the subject is a routing convention, not authentication: trusted credentials and subject permissions still determine who can publish or subscribe. Version the payload contract explicitly, and decide whether a new semantic event needs a new subject rather than changing the meaning silently.

followups.question: Why avoid a subject for every token of generated text?
followups.answer: Subject count is not the only cost; subscriptions, permissions, observability and payload fan-out also need bounds. A coherent subject taxonomy makes routing reviewable. Streaming output can carry bounded sequence metadata without inventing a new authorization surface for every chunk.

followups.question: Can a wildcard subscription cross tenants?
followups.answer: Only if the authenticated principal is granted that subject range. A broad subscription pattern is a request, not proof of permission. Test a credential from tenant A against tenant B subjects and verify denial independently of payload labels.

chapter_title: NATS from subjects to durable consumers
title: Broadcast and worker selection
question: How does a queue group differ from ordinary publish subscribe?
answer: An ordinary matching subscription receives its own live copy. Matching subscribers with the same queue-group name share a copy, with one selected member in that group. Another group can receive another copy. Core NATS does not retain that delivery for redelivery if the selected member crashes; queue membership is load distribution, not a persisted claim or exactly-one business-effect contract. [N4]

In a hypothetical agent system, analytics and an operator dashboard might each need an independent notification, whereas interchangeable cache-refresh workers might share a group. I would not give three independent services the same group name if each must observe every event. I would also avoid treating the selected worker as the durable owner of the business operation. A member can die after receipt or perform an action before losing its response. The POC already expresses ownership through P1 grants and retained original identities. A queue group could choose who tries to wake or inspect work without replacing those authoritative checks.

followups.question: Does one selected member mean exactly one effect?
followups.answer: No. Selection describes routing of this delivery. It says nothing about a handler crash, an application retry, another publication or an external effect. Preserve the original business identity and use its authority to decide what can run.

followups.question: What if one worker is much slower?
followups.answer: Measure outstanding real work and useful completion, then choose bounded concurrency and an appropriate durable work model if needed. Group membership alone is not a fairness, deadline or backpressure policy for arbitrary handler runtimes.

chapter_title: NATS from subjects to durable consumers
title: Request reply does not remove ambiguity
question: How does NATS request reply work, and what does a request timeout tell you?
answer: Request/reply sends a publication with a reply subject and waits for a response under a deadline. Clients commonly use an inbox subscription and correlation internally. A supported no-responders status indicates no known responder interest for that exchange; a timeout leaves delivery/execution uncertain. Neither cancels an earlier request or proves that a database/supplier operation did not happen. [N5]

Suppose a hypothetical specialist receives a request, stores a result and then loses its connection before replying. The requester times out even though useful work happened. Retrying with a fresh work ID could duplicate the operation. I would bind the original scoped command and payload digest, support lookup or original replay where the operation contract permits it, and keep uncertainty visible otherwise. A read-only advisory request may have a simpler retry policy than a supplier mutation. One total deadline should cover the allowed attempts; nested unconditional retries should not multiply work or hide which request identity remains unresolved.

followups.question: Does timeout cancel the responder?
followups.answer: It ends the requester wait. The responder might still be executing or might already have committed. A cancellation protocol needs a separate identity and defined semantics; it cannot be inferred from the disappearance of a reply inbox.

followups.question: Can no responders authorize a new operation key?
followups.answer: It can inform a retry policy for the original attempt, but cannot erase an earlier possibly delivered request. Reconcile the full original operation history. Treat one transport observation as evidence about that exchange, not a global proof of nonexecution.

chapter_title: NATS from subjects to durable consumers
title: The crash gap around consumer acknowledgment
question: When should a durable consumer acknowledge a message?
answer: For an explicit-ACK JetStream consumer, missing acknowledgment can trigger redelivery after AckWait or configured backoff. Retention, MaxDeliver and consumer configuration bound that behavior; it is not an unlimited eventual-processing promise. A confirmed/double ACK lets the client observe that the server recorded its acknowledgment. It still cannot atomically include an application database transaction. [N6, N7]

For a hypothetical projection handler I would atomically retain the original event identity and its derived state in the application database, then acknowledge the delivery. Crash before that transaction means the next delivery can do the work. Crash after commit but before acknowledgment means replay must find the retained identity and avoid another state transition. Acknowledging first creates a loss gap; doing an unprotected external mutation first creates a duplicate-effect gap. If a supplier is involved, use its existing stable effect and reconciliation contract rather than assuming the consumer acknowledgment participates in the supplier transaction.

followups.question: What does double acknowledgment solve?
followups.answer: It reduces uncertainty about whether the broker recorded the consumer ack. It does not atomically include a PostgreSQL write or external supplier call. Keep the application identity ledger so a redelivery remains safe across those separate boundaries.

followups.question: Should every failure be acknowledged?
followups.answer: Define a durable terminal disposition for invalid events, and bounded retry/escalation for transient failures. Reaching MaxDeliver is not an automatic business dead-letter transaction. Retain/quarantine the event and operator evidence under an explicit policy; do not ACK merely to make the pending counter fall.

chapter_title: NATS from subjects to durable consumers
title: Bound exactly once to the right boundary
question: JetStream supports deduplication and confirmed acknowledgments. Why can the application still repeat a side effect?
